era-1931.says: Wikipedia (Flag of India): Congress officially adopted the Swaraj flag with a charkha in 1931; Wikipedia (Historical Indian flags) lists it as saffron, white and green with a blue chakra, 1931-1947. Flags of the World (historical flags of India, from the Anand Bhawan board): at Karachi in March 1931 a committee of seven proposed a plain saffron flag with a charkha, which the AICC rejected; a resolution then adopted a saffron-white-green tricolour with a blue charkha in 1931, with colour meanings courage and sacrifice, truth and peace, faith and chivalry. FOTW's country page adds that the tricolour had been used unofficially since the early 1920s.
era-1931.open: The exact day of the 1931 resolution differs within FOTW (1 August on the board, first hoisted 31 August; one contributor gives August 1933); the wheel colour is blue in the description but reddish in the board's picture.

era-1921.says: Wikipedia (Flag of India): Gandhi proposed a flag with a charkha in Young India in April 1921; red for Hindus and green for Muslims at first, white added later; secular meanings given in 1929; endorsed by Congress in July 1923. Flags of the World (historical flags of India): at Bezwada on 31 March 1921 an Andhra youth made a red and green flag for Gandhi, who added a white strip and a charkha; it became popular at Congress sessions but was never officially accepted (a second FOTW page credits Pingali Venkayya's design, modified by Gandhi).
era-1921.open: The two sources differ on the date (April 1921 in Young India vs 31 March at Bezwada) and on the colour order; whether the 1921 wheel was yellow or another colour differs in the pictures FOTW shows.

era-1917.says: Wikipedia (Flag of India) dates the Home Rule flag to 1916, adopted by Besant and Tilak, with the Union Jack canton, a star and crescent, seven stars, five red and four green bands; Wikipedia (Historical Indian flags) lists it as 1917. Flags of the World (two pages) dates it to 1917 (one page labels the illustration 1916), same design, associated with Annie Besant and Tilak.
era-1917.open: The year is 1916 or 1917 depending on the source; the meaning of the Union Jack canton as a dominion-status claim appears only in Wikipedia's Historical Indian flags, unsourced; the Coimbatore ban is from Wikipedia only.

era-1906.says: Wikipedia (Flag of India): a flag linked to the 1905 partition of Bengal with eight lotuses, a sun and crescent, and Vande Mataram on a central band; no designer or launch date. Flags of the World (historical flags of India, citing Singh, Nair and the Congress website): the Calcutta flag with eight lotuses, Vande Mataram in Devanagari and a sun, crescent and star, reportedly first hoisted on 7 August 1906 at Parsee Bagan, Calcutta; designers disputed.
era-1906.open: Band order and colours differ between the sources (FOTW: red, yellow, green; Wikipedia: green, yellow, red); the designer and exact hoisting are disputed; the page's Anandamath link is not in either source.

era-1858.says: Wikipedia (Flag of British India): a Red Ensign with the Union Jack in the canton and the Star of India in the fly, the Civil Ensign of British India 1880-1947; Wikipedia (Historical Indian flags) also lists a Blue Ensign with the Star of India for the Royal Indian Marine, 1863-1947. Flags of the World (British Rule in India): the Blue Ensign with the Star of India badge became the ensign of H.M. Indian Marine in 1879, a Red Ensign with the badge was a semi-official land flag, and the Viceroy flew the Union Flag with the badge from c.1885 to 1947.
era-1858.open: The field colour depends on the use: red for the civil ensign, blue for the marine ensign; the card shows the blue form. Dates for the blue ensign differ (1863 on Wikipedia, 1879 on FOTW). How widely these flags flew on land is not stated.

era-1757.says: Flags of the World (East India Company flags): red and white horizontal stripes, usually thirteen, with a canton that carried the Union flag from about 1707 and the 1801 Union flag afterwards; the Company ceased operations in 1864. Wikipedia (Flag of the British East India Company): red and white stripes with a canton changing from the English flag to the Great Britain flag and, from 1801, the Union Flag; the Company was nationalised in 1858 and its flag lost official status.
era-1757.open: Neither source states use on forts; FOTW says the ensign was restricted to eastern waters from 1676; the claimed link to the US flag has no written evidence per Wikipedia.

era-1707.says: Wikipedia (Flags of the Mughal Empire): the imperial standard (alam) was primarily moss green with a lion and sun facing the hoist, other paintings show scarlet or green fields; it does not date the standard to 1707-1857. Flags of the World (India before British rule): imperial standard and emperor's flag both with a lion and the sun behind it, a simplified army banner; no dates.
era-1707.open: Both sources show a lion with the sun, not the plain gold star on the card. Neither says the banner was used, or faded, between 1707 and 1857. Page text hedged accordingly.

era-1526.says: Wikipedia (Flags of the Mughal Empire): the imperial standard (alam) was primarily moss green with a lion and sun facing the hoist, traced to Timur; a Padshahnama painting shows green fields with a couchant lion and rising sun and a 17th-century caption describes a green standard with a gold sun. Flags of the World (India before British rule): imperial standard and emperor's flag with a lion and the sun behind it.
era-1526.open: Both sources agree on a lion-and-sun emblem, green predominating on Wikipedia, so the card's plain gold star on green is not what they describe; neither gives a 1526-1707 date range for a single flag. Left unreviewed until the card is redrawn.

era-1206.says: Wikipedia (Delhi Sultanate): the infobox shows a flag 'according to the contemporary Catalan Atlas (c. 1375)', with no design described. Wikipedia (Historical Indian flags): the Catalan Atlas flag, a grey flag with a black strip left of centre, dated 1320-1413 and attributed to the Tughlaq dynasty, with the note that there is no evidence it was actually used by the Delhi Sultanate (citing Kadoi 2010). Flags of the World (India before British rule) does not cover the Sultanate.
era-1206.open: No source supports the dark red field with a gold crescent on the card, which the page already calls a reconstruction; no flag for the 1206-1320 or 1413-1526 dynasties is covered.

era-322bce.says: Wikipedia (Flag of India): the Ashoka Chakra comes from the Lion Capital of Ashoka. Wikipedia (Maurya Empire): Nehru proposed in July 1947 that the 24-pointed Buddhist Wheel of Dharma on the Lion Capital at Sarnath be the central feature of the national flag. FOTW (India): the wheel is the wheel of the law of the 3rd-century BC Maurya emperor Ashoka. Flags of the World (India before British rule) has nothing on the Maurya.
era-322bce.open: Neither Wikipedia nor FOTW says the Maurya used any flag; the 24-spoke wheel on the pillar is documented, but the card is a reconstruction of the pillar, not a banner. Only the part of the Maurya article before character 100,000 was read.

era-320.says: Wikipedia (Gupta Empire) describes Garuda on Gupta coins and seals (a Kumaragupta I coin reverse shows Garuda standing with spread wings; Ramagupta coin types include a Garuda and a Garudadhvaja type) but mentions no Gupta flag and no wheel on coinage. FOTW (India) does not mention a Gupta flag.
era-320.open: The Garuda motif is supported by Wikipedia; the wheel (chakra) motif on coinage and any Gupta banner are not in the sources read. Only the part of the Gupta article before character 100,000 was read.

era-1949.says: Wikipedia: hoisted 27 December 1949 on transfer of sovereignty; made official 17 August 1950; Law 24/2009. FOTW: Law 24 of 2009 gives RGB values; flag adopted 17 August 1945.

era-1527.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-650.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1945.says: Wikipedia: 17 August 1945 flag introduced and hoisted in Jakarta; Bendera Pusaka sewn by Fatmawati; 1920s revival; first flown in Java in 1928 and banned. FOTW: independence proclaimed 17 August 1945 and the flag raised; 1922 Leiden banteng flag; 1928 PNI; 1929 plain flag.
era-1945.open: The sources differ on when the plain flag was first raised (1928 vs 1929).

era-1293.says: Wikipedia: colours linked to the Majapahit banner (infobox 11 November 1293). FOTW: based on a Majapahit flag with nine red and white stripes.
era-1293.open: The name 'Gula Kelapa' is in neither source.

era-1942.says: Wikipedia (Japanese occupation of the Dutch East Indies): the infobox flag, captioned 'Flag of Japanese-occupied Dutch East Indies', is the Japanese flag; the ban on the Indonesian flag and anthem was not lifted when Japanese leaders met independence figures in 1943, and after Koiso's promise of 7 September 1944 authorities in Java allowed the Indonesian flag at Jawa Hokokai buildings. Flags of the World (Indonesia): the first flag was flown 'amidst Japanese occupation forces' at the 17 August 1945 proclamation (official history), and Mark Sensen thinks most Dutch flags did not survive the occupation.
era-1942.open: The Japanese flag as the occupation's flag and the ban on the Indonesian flag rest on Wikipedia alone; Flags of the World does not describe the occupation's flag, and neither source describes a naval or military ensign.

era-1800.says: Wikipedia (Dutch East Indies): the infobox flag is captioned 'Flag of Dutch East Indies' and is the Dutch tricolour, with the Japanese occupation dated 1942-1945; the flag of Indonesia article dates Dutch use to 1 January 1800 - 27 December 1949 and says the red-white flag first flown in Java in 1928 was quickly prohibited. Flags of the World (Indonesia): the Leiden students adopted a red-over-white flag in 1922, the first plain red-over-white flag was hoisted at a Batavia student congress in 1929, and the PNI hoisted it in Bandung in 1928; it names the Dutch flags (nl.html) as the colonial power's flags.
era-1800.open: Flags of the World does not state that the Dutch tricolour was the colony's flag, so that rests on Wikipedia alone; neither source says whether the colonial state had its own ensign; the page's end date 1942 differs from Wikipedia's 1949.

era-1602.says: Wikipedia (Dutch East India Company, first 100,000 of 226,976 characters): the infobox flag is captioned 'Company flag (1630)' and the text says the VOC monogram (a large V with an O on the left and a C on the right) appeared on corporate items such as flags, cannons and coins, without saying the flag bore it; Wikipedia's Flag of Indonesia dates the Company flag 20 March 1602 - 1 January 1800. Flags of the World's Indonesia and Netherlands pages do not mention the VOC.
era-1602.open: The monogram on a Dutch tricolour as the flag over the whole 1602-1800 span is not confirmed by text in any source read; only one publisher (Wikipedia) is available, and the 1602 versus 1603 start date is unresolved.

era-1979.says: Wikipedia: Interim Government removed the crown from the naval ensign in 1979; older flags stayed in use until 1980; current flag adopted July 1980, designed by Hamid Nadimi, Takbir 11 times on each band, 22 in total. FOTW: traditional flags abolished after the shah's abdication in 1979; 22 refers to the victory of the revolution on 22 Bahman 1357.
era-1979.open: The sources give only July 1980; the 'tulip' reading of the emblem is not in either.

era-1925.says: Wikipedia: 14 August 1905 first official flag; 7 October 1907 laws describe a green, white and red tricolour with a lion and sun; 1933 colours darkened and sun altered; 1964 ratio 1:3 to 4:7. FOTW: tricolour first designed 1907.
era-1925.open: The 1933 'fixed in law' wording is not in either source.

era-1789.says: Wikipedia: late Fath-Ali Shah lion and sun on flags and coins; 14 August 1905; 7 October 1907 tricolour with a lion and sun. FOTW: tricolour first designed in 1907.
era-1789.open: The 'about 1910' date and the plain-colour early banners are not in the sources.

era-1501.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Iran): the lion and sun became Iran's recognised emblem by the time of Shah Abbas. Wikipedia (Safavid Iran): the infobox flag is captioned 'Flag of Safavid Empire (1576-1732)' with no design described, and the Qizilbash banner and lion and sun are not mentioned in the part read. FOTW's Iran page has no Safavid page.
era-1501.open: No source read describes a green Safavid state banner; the plain green field is the page's own approximation.

era-1736.says: Wikipedia describes Afsharid flags (1736-1747) such as a white naval flag with a red sword, and an undated Zand pennant of white with a green border and a gold lion and sun. Wikipedia's Safavid Iran article does not mention the Zand dynasty and shows Afsharid Iran only as a navigation link.
era-1736.open: No second source on Afsharid or Zand flags was found; FOTW's Iran page has no historical sub-pages and links Encyclopaedia Iranica's flags article, which was not fetched; the 'solid-colour banners with a sun emblem' wording is unsupported.

era-651.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Iran): the Seljuk flag was most probably black like the Abbasid flag. Wikipedia (Abbasid Caliphate): the Abbasid 'Black Standard' was the sign under which Abu Muslim began the Khurasan revolt (747); the Abbasid Caliphate is dated 750-1258 and the Umayyads 661-750; no Umayyad white banner is mentioned.
era-651.open: The Black Standard is documented only from the Abbasid revolt of 747-750, so it does not fit the 651-750 part of this era (Rashidun and Umayyad rule); no source read describes a banner for Iran 651-747 or for 750-819.

era-224.says: Wikipedia: Derafsh Kaviani was the official Sasanian standard (224-651); Shapur Shahbazi describes a heavily jewelled purple background, a star emblem and tassels in red, gold and purple; known images are artistic renditions (a 17th-century Safavid miniature, a 1948 painting, a modern illustration); the apron legend is Iranian mythology.
era-224.open: Wikipedia's Flag of Iran article and FOTW do not cover it; Wikipedia does not name the Shahnameh as the legend's source, and does not state that nothing survives.

era-2008.says: Wikipedia: approved by the Council of Representatives on 22 January 2008 (Law 9 of 2008), three stars removed, takbir in bold dark green Kufic script. FOTW: parliament voted on 22 January 2008 for the act that removed the three stars and kept the green Kufic takbir (described as interim for one year).

era-1963.says: Wikipedia: three-star flag adopted 31 July 1963 under Law 28 of 1963 by the government of Abdul Salam Arif. Flags of the World (Iraq evolution page): the 1963-1991 flag is dated 31 July 1963 - 13 January 1991; three red-white-black stripes with three green stars on the white stripe; the stars were meant to remind Iraqis of attempts to unify Arab countries (Egypt, Syria), later reinterpreted as the Baath motto after the 1968 coup (a contributor, citing a site no longer online).
era-1963.open: The two sources name different governments (Wikipedia: Arif's; Flags of the World contributor: the Baathist government); the colour description in FOTW is inferred from the UAR flag rather than stated for 1963.

era-1991.says: Wikipedia: in January 1991, during the Gulf War, Saddam Hussein added the takbir between the stars (the page gives 13 or 14 January from different sources; amending law dated 22 January 1991) and says its form 'was said to be Saddam's own handwriting'. FOTW: takbir added 13 January 1991, with comments saying it was in Saddam's handwriting. Wikipedia also records a transitional Kufic-script version unveiled 28 July 2004 with the three stars retained, so the flag was not unchanged until 2008.
era-1991.open: The exact 1991 day differs between sources; the 2004 Kufic version falls inside this span.

era-1958.says: Wikipedia and Flags of the World (Iraqi Republic 1959-1963, citing Alexander & Smith 1992) agree that the republic's flag adopted a year after the July 1958 revolution (Wikipedia: Law 102 of 1959) was a black-white-green flag with an eight-pointed star containing a circle in the middle (Flags of the World: the 'Sun of Mesopotamia', star red, yellow core for the Kurds and red rays for the Christian-Assyrians). Wikipedia also lists a February-July 1958 Arab Federation flag.
era-1958.open: The two sources agree on the real design, but this page's drawing and caption (a sun-and-dagger device on red-white-black bands) match neither, so the row cannot be attested until the drawing is replaced; FOTW describes the bands as vertical while Wikipedia's text was not compared on that point; no flag for the 1958 revolution itself (July 1958 - 1959) is described.

era-1932.says: Flags of the World (Kingdom of Iraq 1924-1958, quoting Art. 4 of the 1925 Constitution) describes a black-white-green horizontal tricolour with a red trapezoid at the hoist carrying two white seven-pointed stars, adopted 10 July 1924 (Bruce Berry) and in use at independence in 1932; Wikipedia gives the same 10 July 1924 date and design. Both therefore agree the 1932 flag was the 1924 design.
era-1932.open: The two sources agree on the design and the 1924 date, but this page's drawing shows a single star, which matches neither; FOTW's page gives 1924-1959 in text and 1924-1958 in its title; row stays unreviewed until the drawing is corrected.

era-1920.says: Flags of the World (Mesopotamia 1920-1924) says 'Sources do not agree about the flags used in Iraq during this period': Alexander & Smith give a two-star flag for 1920-21 and the same flag without stars from 1921 to 1924, while Smith (1975) shows a starless black-white-green flag with a red triangle. Wikipedia gives a starless 1921 flag used from 23 August 1921 to 10 July 1924. The two publishers agree on no star for 1921-24; neither mentions British flags.
era-1920.open: This page's white seven-pointed star in 1921 is contradicted by both; FOTW does not name Faisal as designer or use the term British Mandate; the mandate start (1920) and the 1921 adoption date are not tied to a flag by FOTW. Row stays unreviewed until the drawing matches.

era-1534.says: Flags of the World's Iraq index lists 'Ottoman Empire c. 1535-1920' (tr-ottom.html) as the historical flag entry for Iraq in that span; Wikipedia (Flag of the Ottoman Empire) describes a simple crescent flag in early centuries, an eight-pointed star decree for naval ships in 1793, and the five-pointed version officially adopted in 1844 (footnote: 1826 under Mahmud II). Flags of the World's Ottoman page gives 1793 and 1844 from Zanamierowski, flagged as unevidenced.
era-1534.open: Neither source describes an Iraq-specific provincial flag; the sultan for 1844 is not named; Ottoman 1844 date is contested (1826); the 1534 start is close to the FOTW 1535 date.

era-762.says: Wikipedia (Abbasid Caliphate): the infobox flag is captioned 'The Abbasid Black Standard'; Abu Muslim began the revolt under the Black Standard; al-Mansur founded Baghdad in 762 (capital 762-836 and 892-1258); the caliphate effectively ended with the Mongol sack of Baghdad in 1258. Flags of the World (religious flags) says the Abbasid Revolution adopted black for its rayah, but this is pasted from Wikipedia plus a contributor's uncited belief that a white Shahada was shown.
era-762.open: Both publishers trace to Wikipedia, so there is no independent second source; the claim that black remained the caliphate's recognised state colour through 1258 is not stated by either.

era-637.says: Flags of the World (religious flags) quotes Wikipedia that Ali used the Prophet's white liwa at Siffin and that forces loyal to Marwan II adopted red; it never names the Umayyads. Ronart (1959) is cited only for the caliphate being spiritual, political and military leadership.
era-637.open: No independent source states a white Umayyad banner or its use in Iraq; the 637 conquest date and Rashidun banners are not covered.

era-1949.says: Wikipedia quotes Article 7 of the 1937 Constitution: «The national flag is the tricolour of green, white and orange». FOTW says the tricolour was adopted as the national flag in 1937, confirmed on 29 December 1937. Wikipedia gives the Department of the Taoiseach's reading of the colours (green for Catholics, orange for Protestants, white for peace) and Meagher's 1848 explanation.
era-1949.open: The sources date the flag's status to 1937 (and its use to 1922); 1949 is the Republic's start, not a flag event.

era-1171-1.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1922.says: Wikipedia says the Executive Council adopted the tricolour for the Free State without contest and without statute, as a provisional decision (all citation-needed), and that Article 7 of the 1937 Constitution confirmed it. FOTW says the tricolour was used almost entirely within the Free State in 1922–39 and often called the Sinn Féin flag, that the Defence Forces adopted orange as the third colour in 1923, and that a 1928 government document said the government had taken over the «Free State flag» to forestall republican use.
era-1922.open: This page used to say it was formally adopted at independence; the sources say it was taken up without statute and confirmed in 1937.

era-1919.says: Wikipedia says the flag was adopted by the Irish Republic during the War of Independence (citation needed) and, for 1916, that the tricolour was raised over the GPO, that a green harp flag also flew, and that the Irish Republic flag was treated as a banner rather than the national flag. FOTW dates Meagher's unveiling to 7 March 1848 in Waterford, earlier than the 15 April 1848 date formerly given.
era-1919.open: The GPO flags are from 1916, which is before this era. Wikipedia's April 1848 date and FOTW's 7 March 1848 differ.

era-1541.says: Wikipedia (Kingdom of Ireland): the Kingdom 'had no official flag or arms' though numerous flags of Ireland existed; a Royal Standard of Ireland is captioned 1542-1801; the arms are azure a harp Or. Wikipedia (Flag of Ireland): a green flag with a harp was used by Eoghan Ruadh O Neill in 1642 and by the Catholic Confederation in the 1640s. FOTW: a gold harp on green is the traditional Green Flag of Ireland (undated); its Lordship page calls the earlier three-crowns banner non-historical.
era-1541.open: The Kingdom is dated 1542 in Wikipedia's Kingdom article (this page says 1541); no source calls a green harp flag a flag of the Kingdom itself; Henry VIII's replacement of the three-crowns arms is not covered.

era-1171.says: Wikipedia says a commission of Edward IV of about 1467–68 blazoned the arms as «Azure, three crowns in pale Or, bordure Argent» (Kennedy, 1991), that their origin may lie with Irish magnates in Edward I's Scottish wars about 1300, and that the Dukedom of Ireland of 1386 may be linked.
era-1171.open: Arms, not a flag; no source says they were flown as one. The reason for abandoning them is called speculative.

era-1801.says: FOTW (United Kingdom): the Union Flag was adopted 1 January 1801, adding St Patrick's saltire for Ireland after the Union with Ireland Act 1800, on top of the 1606 flag combining England and Scotland. Wikipedia (Union Jack): the design dates from 1 January 1801 and was not changed after the Irish Free State was established in December 1922.
era-1801.open: Neither source describes how the flag was used in Ireland between 1801 and 1919, or the 'governed directly from Westminster' framing; the saltire's origin is given by Wikipedia as the FitzGerald arms.

era-1948.says: Both sources give 1948, the year this page starts the current flag. Wikipedia's infobox gives the adoption as 1885; Flags of the World dates it 28 October 1948.
era-1948.open: Only the year the current flag was adopted was compared; the design and the swatch colours were not checked against a specification.

era-1917.says: Wikipedia (Mandatory Palestine): the infobox shows the Union Flag as the flag of Palestine for 1920-1948. Flags of the World (Palestine historical flags): the British took Jerusalem in December 1916 and a Union Flag variant was used for Palestine and Transjordan 1916-1923; the mandate was created 25 April 1920 and approved 24 July 1922. Flags of the World (Mandate of Palestine 1922-1948): a Union Flag is shown and nothing was done about a flag as a special badge was not thought desirable; a defaced Red Ensign was authorised in 1927 and a PALESTINE Blue Ensign in 1929. Flags of the World (history of the national flag): the Zionist flag had no official standing (Karner 2023).
era-1917.open: Neither source describes how the Union Flag was flown in practice; the 1916-1923 'variant' is not described in text; the 15 May 1948 cancellation of departmental flags matches the page's end date.

era-1517.says: Wikipedia (Ottoman Syria): infobox shows the Flag of the Ottoman Empire for 1516-1918 and says Palestine was part of Syria (the mutessarriflik of Jerusalem and parts of the vilayets of Beirut and Syria). Flags of the World (Palestine historical flags, Dotor 2000): Palestine 'was part of the Ottoman Empire and used the Ottoman flag', with the image captioned 'Ottoman Palestine until 1916'. Flags of the World (Jerusalem civil ensign): the Ottomans had authority over the Holy Land until 1918.
era-1517.open: No source describes a provincial flag of Palestine under the Ottomans, and the design of the Ottoman flag before 1793 or 1844 is contested (see the Ottoman Empire page of this atlas); Flags of the World ends Ottoman Palestine at 1916, Wikipedia at 1918, and this page at 1917.

era-1291.says: Wikipedia (Mamluk Sultanate): 1250-1517 state in Egypt, Hejaz and Syria; Mamluks entered Palestine and routed the Mongols in 1260; the infobox gives no flag, and the article's 'Emblems and blazons' section lay beyond the first 100,000 of 265,448 characters read. Flags of the World's Israel historical index (il_his) has no Mamluk entry; its Jerusalem civil ensign page covers the Franciscan ensign from 1333 without naming the Mamluks.
era-1291.open: The Mamluk gold field with an eagle blazon is not described by any source read; the unread Wikipedia emblems section is the place to check next.

era-1099.says: Flags of the World (Kingdom of Jerusalem 1099-1291): white flag with a large yellow cross potent and four yellow crosslets (the Jerusalem cross), blazon 'Argent, a cross potent between four crosslets or' (Fox-Davies 1996); per Smith 1975 Baldwin III used a plain white flag and the yellow cross was added by Amalric I (1162-1173). Wikipedia (Kingdom of Jerusalem): the infobox flag is captioned 'Flag of Latin Jerusalem' and the royal banner and arms link to the Jerusalem cross; the kingdom ran from Godfrey's accession in 1099 to the fall of Acre in 1291.
era-1099.open: Flags of the World dates the addition of the cross to 1162-1173 for the royal flag, later than 1099; Wikipedia's text does not describe the banner and the infobox link is unexplained; the crosslet form is disputed (Smith versus Fox-Davies and Neubecker).

era-636.says: Wikipedia (Umayyad Caliphate and Fatimid Caliphate, first 100,000 characters each) describe the Umayyad conquest of Syria and Palestine under Umar and the Fatimid retaking of Ramla in May 972, but neither describes a banner or flag. Flags of the World's historical index for Israel has no Umayyad or Fatimid entry.
era-636.open: The white Umayyad and green Fatimid colours are not stated by any source read for this region; the remaining ~200,000 characters of each Wikipedia article were not read.

era-1946.says: FOTW says the plain tricolour, without arms, has been used since 19 June 1946 and officially since 1 January 1948. Wikipedia's infobox lists the flag as adopted with the founding of the Republic (18 June 1946) and says Article 12 of the Constitution defines it as a vertical tricolour of green, white and red; the civil flag variant is dated 9 November 1948.
era-1946.open: The 1946 decree text was not read. The two sources differ by a day on the 1946 date, and by two years on when it became official.

era-1032.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1861.says: Wikipedia says the Kingdom of Italy was proclaimed on 17 March 1861, the tricolour became its national flag, and the 1861–1946 state flag was defaced with the arms of Savoy and a crown. FOTW says the flag with the Savoy arms on the white stripe was the Kingdom of Sardinia's flag and «later (1861)» the Kingdom of Italy's.
era-1861.open: The design of the crowned shield in 1861 is not described by either source beyond this.

era-1848.says: Wikipedia says that about 23 March 1848 Charles Albert said his troops would carry a tricolour with the Savoy arms superimposed on the white. FOTW says the flag with the Savoy arms on the white stripe was the Kingdom of Sardinia's flag from 1848.
era-1848.open: Neither source mentions the Statuto's flag decree that this page cites; a 1999 FOTW discussion says a Sardinian ship could not have displayed the tricolour before 1848, and that it may have been in popular but unofficial use.

era-1814.says: FOTW (Kingdom of Sardinia part 2): the state flag was adopted by letters patent on 30 December 1814 with a blue border, a red canton bearing white and red crosses, and a crown, and was superseded on 15 April 1848; another contributor says only the royal standard (white with a blue border) was used from about 1814 to 1848. Wikipedia (Kingdom of Sardinia): naval flags used a blue flag with the Savoy cross in one canton; Wikipedia (Flag of Italy): blue was the dynastic colour.
era-1814.open: The sources do not support this page's plain blue field with a white cross; FOTW's account is contributor notes from a single publisher and Wikipedia does not describe the pre-1848 state flag.

era-1416.says: FOTW: the traditional flag of Savoy is red with a white cross, blazoned 'de gueules a la croix d'argent', in use 'since the Middle Ages'. Wikipedia (Flag of Italy): the Savoy arms are gules a cross argent (later fimbriated azure); Wikipedia (County of Savoy): Savoy was raised to a duchy in 1416 by King Sigismund.
era-1416.open: Neither source gives a 14th-century date or states that the flag was used continuously; the page's later description of this flag as 'blue Savoy-cross' (Kingdom of Sardinia era) is a separate, unconfirmed claim.

era-1945.says: Wikipedia: 17 March 1861 tricolour with Savoy arms; the Republic ended the Kingdom's flag on 18 June 1946 (a decree of 19 June 1946 removed the Savoy arms). FOTW: Savoy shield with a crown over it on the state flag and war ensign in 1861; plain tricolour the Republic's flag from 19 June 1946; its Kingdom of Italy page says only 'green white red with Savoy arms'.
era-1945.open: The June 1944 removal of the crown is in neither source (Wikipedia, read for the Salo section, mentions no 1944 change to the Savoy arms), so the crownless shield drawn here is unconfirmed.

era-1943.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Italy): the Salo national flag was identical to the modern Republic's plain tricolour and its war flag bore a silver or black eagle and fascio littorio. FOTW: the Salo Republic's state flag was the plain tricolour and its war flag a Roman eagle (black in official descriptions) grasping fasces, per Decree No. 141 of 28 January 1944.
era-1943.open: FOTW's decree text also puts a republican fasces on the flagstaff of the state flag, and the colour of the eagle and fasces varies between descriptions; the page's propaganda framing is not covered.

era-1922.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Italy): Law no. 2264 of 24 December 1925 made the tricolour the national flag of the Kingdom; in 1926 a proposal to add the fasces to the flag was stopped by strong monarchist opposition. FOTW does not cover the fascist period.
era-1922.open: Wikipedia says the 1926 fasces proposal was blocked, which conflicts with this page's statement that the fasces were added to the flag by law in 1926; no source read documents a fasces added to the state flag.

era-1798.says: Wikipedia (Kingdom of Sardinia): on 6 December 1798 Joubert occupied Turin and forced Charles Emmanuel IV to abdicate; the mainland domains were occupied and eventually annexed by Napoleonic France while Cagliari was the de facto seat of the exiled Savoy court until 1814. Wikipedia and FOTW on Italy cover the Cisalpine and Napoleonic tricolours of other states.
era-1798.open: No source read states that the French tricolour flew over Piedmont or that a Savoy flag survived on Sardinia in this period.

era-1720.says: Wikipedia (Kingdom of Sardinia): the Treaty of The Hague of 17 February 1720 formalised the exchange giving Savoy the Sardinian crown; Wikipedia (Flag of Italy) shows Piedmont-Sardinia flags only from 1848 and gives the Savoy arms as a white cross on red edged in blue. FOTW (Duchy of Savoy): a 1785 flag with a very thin blue border and an undated blue flag with a red canton bearing the white cross.
era-1720.open: No source documents a plain blue Savoy flag for the kingdom in 1720-1798; FOTW's 1785 and blue-with-canton flags are single-publisher and differ from the page's drawing.

era-1962.says: Both sources give 1962, the year this page starts the current flag. Wikipedia's infobox gives the adoption as 6 August 1962; Flags of the World dates it 6 August 1962.
era-1962.open: Only the year the current flag was adopted was compared; the design and the swatch colours were not checked against a specification.

era-650.says: This page's own caption calls the image a placeholder: «placeholder — Taino chiefdoms, no flag survives».
era-650.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1875.says: Wikipedia shows a historical flag image labelled 1875-1906. Flags of the World (Jamaica colonial flags, citing Prothero and the 1881 HMSO list of colonial badges): in 1875 the arms became the flag badge on the Blue Ensign and the Union Jack, the 1875 badge having an oval shield with St George's cross and five gold pineapples; the badge was replaced in 1906, again by a new grant in 1957, and both flags were discontinued on 6 August 1962.
era-1875.open: Wikipedia gives no description of the 1875 flag; the badge changed in 1906 and 1957, and the card shows a simplified badge; FOTW notes Red Ensigns of this design were unofficial and undated.

era-1655.says: Flags of the World (Jamaica): John McGhie's opinion that the colonial flag was of course the Union Jack, in some form; (Jamaica colonial flags) the Union Jack with the badge is documented only from 1875 to 1906 and the page gives no 1655 start. Wikipedia's article on Jamaica's flag does not cover 1655-1875.
era-1655.open: Use of a plain Union Flag from 1655 and the absence of a badge before 1875 are not stated by any source; FOTW notes arms were granted in 1661.

era-1509.says: Wikipedia (Spanish Jamaica) dates the colony 1509-1655 and mentions no flag; Wikipedia (Cross of Burgundy flag) says the flag served as the flag of the Viceroyalties of the New World after Habsburg officials introduced it in the Americas from 1506; Flags of the World (Cross of Burgundy) says it was never the official flag of the Spanish Empire but a military banner, with flags bearing the cross from 1518, and that it was uncertain whether conquistadors carried it.
era-1509.open: No source ties the Cross of Burgundy to Jamaica, and the two publishers disagree on whether it was an official colonial flag.

era-1945.says: Wikipedia (Occupation of Japan): flying the Hinomaru was initially severely restricted (individuals and prefectural offices could apply for permission), partially lifted in 1948 and completely lifted the following year; Wikipedia (Flag of Japan): MacArthur lifted some limits in May 1947 and general restrictions ended in January 1949. FOTW: a modified signal flag 'E' replaced the Hinomaru as the Japanese merchant ensign from 2 September 1945 until 31 March 1952.
era-1945.open: Wikipedia's two articles differ on the first easing (May 1947 vs 1948); the occupation lasted to April 1952, beyond this era's 1947 end date on the page.

era-1868.says: Wikipedia: Proclamation 57 of 27 February 1870 for merchant ships; 16-ray rising sun war flag 15 May 1870; Imperial Japanese Navy ensign 1889–1945. FOTW: Proclamation 57 of 27 January 1870; army 16-ray flag gazetted 13 June 1870; Proclamation 651 naval flag with centred disc; 8 October 1889 new set of flags.
era-1868.open: The two sources differ on 27 January or 27 February 1870 and on the naval gazette date.

era-1603.says: FOTW: the shogunate adopted the sun flag for its ships in the early 1600s. Wikipedia: in 1854 ships were ordered to fly the Hinomaru.
era-1603.open: The sources do not mention clan mon.

era-1336.says: FOTW (feudal flags): in the period of war among the states (1467-1603) each of 68 kuni was ruled by a daimyo with colourful flags based on mon (hata-sashimono); Ashikaga held the shogun title 1336-1573. Wikipedia (Flag of Japan): the oldest existing flag, at Unpo-ji, is older than the 16th century; at Nagashino (28 June 1575) Oda Nobunaga, Tokugawa Ieyasu and Takeda Katsuyori each had flags with family crests and both sides also raised the Hinomaru, which Wikipedia reads as use as a national symbol.
era-1336.open: FOTW supports clan flags only from 1467 (not 1336-1467), and Wikipedia's account of both armies raising the Hinomaru in 1575 cuts against 'no unified national flag'; nothing read describes flags for 1336-1467.

era-1185.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Japan): the Taira (red flag with gold circle) and Minamoto (white flag with red circle) used sun-disc banners in the Genpei War (1180-1185) and later warlords noted the Hinomaru's value; Nichiren is said to have given a sun banner to the shogun in the Mongol invasions of the 13th century. Wikipedia (Genpei War): red and white, the colours of the Taira and Minamoto standards, were established as Japan's national colours. FOTW (Japan): the same Nichiren story, with the words 'it is said'.
era-1185.open: The Nichiren sun banner is a legend in both Wikipedia and FOTW; neither source describes the flags actually flown under the Kamakura shogunate, and the claim that no national flag existed is a negative that no source states.

era-794.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Japan): the Shoku Nihongi records a sun-motif flag (the golden-sun Nissho) at Emperor Monmu's New Year ceremony in 701; until the Heian period the Nishiki flag of the Imperial Court had a golden sun and a silver moon on red; at the end of the Heian era the Taira used a red flag with a gold circle and the Minamoto a white flag with a red circle (Genpei War 1180-1185). The same article calls the Unpo-ji flag the oldest existing flag.
era-794.open: Only Wikipedia's Flag of Japan covers this era (its Genpei War article adds only the national-colours remark); no second publisher or reference source was found in FOTW's Japanese pages for the Heian period.

era-1946.says: Both sources date the current flag to 1928, before this era begins in 1946, so the flag was already in use at the start. Wikipedia's infobox gives the adoption as 16 April 1928; Flags of the World dates it April 1928.
era-1946.open: Only the year the current flag was adopted was compared; the design and the swatch colours were not checked against a specification.

era-1921.says: Wikipedia (Flag of the Arab Revolt): a gallery lists the Emirate of Transjordan as using the Hejaz (Arab Revolt) flag 1921-1928 and a flag of its own for 1928-1939; Wikipedia (Emirate of Transjordan): infobox flags captioned 1922-1939 and 1939-1946, no design given, no mention of Mandate flag use. FOTW: contributors disagree on the 1921 flag (star or none; star added 1928) and the British Mandate of Palestine used the Union Flag.
era-1921.open: No source read says the Union Flag flew over Transjordan; the sources instead point to Hashemite flags of black, white and green with a red triangle. The page's Union Flag drawing is therefore not confirmed.

era-1517.says: FOTW: before 1916 Jordan was part of the Ottoman Empire and used the Ottoman flag. Wikipedia (Flag of the Ottoman Empire): crescent flags appeared from 1453, a red flag with a white eight-pointed star and crescent was the official state flag 1793-1844, and a five-pointed-star version was adopted in 1844.
era-1517.open: Neither source describes flags specific to the Syrian or Transjordan provinces, and the design varied across the 400 years of this era (earlier flags included Zulfiqar-sword war flags), so the single crescent-and-star shown is correct only for roughly 1793-1916.

era-1260.says: Neither Wikipedia's nor FOTW's Jordan flag pages describe a Mamluk flag for this region. Wikipedia's Mamluk Sultanate article (first 100,000 characters read) mentions al-Karak only as a place of exile and does not describe the sultanate's emblems in the part read; FOTW's page eg-mam.html returned 404.
era-1260.open: The Mamluk eagle blazon and gold field are unsourced reconstruction; the 'Emblems and blazons' section of Wikipedia's Mamluk article was not reached and no regional banner is documented.

era-1189.says: Neither source describes Ayyubid banners; the Abbasid, Umayyad and Fatimid dynasties appear only as sources of the modern flag's colours. No Ayyubid-specific page was found on FOTW.
era-1189.open: Not looked up beyond the Jordan pages: a source on Ayyubid banners (a yellow banner is commonly stated) was not read, so the plain dark field remains a placeholder.

era-1115.says: Wikipedia (Lordship of Oultrejordain): the lordship ran from c. 1118 to 1189 (infobox 1118-1187), with Baldwin I's castle at Montreal in 1115; the article describes no banner, arms or Jerusalem cross for it. Neither Jordan flag page mentions it.
era-1115.open: The Jerusalem cross attribution is unsourced; the 1115 start date is the castle's, the lordship being dated c. 1118.

era-636.says: Wikipedia and FOTW give black as an Abbasid colour and white as an Umayyad colour, as symbolism of the modern flag; neither describes banners flown in this period.
era-636.open: No source documents an Umayyad or Abbasid banner for Jund al-Urdunn; the plain white is a representative choice.

era-1991.says: Wikipedia's infobox gives the adoption of the current flag as 4 June 1992; FOTW's header gives 'Flag adopted 1992-JUNE-4' and cites the law of 4 June 1992 (a later section on the law says 4 July 1992). FOTW also lists a first variant and 1992 proposals.
era-1991.open: The era starts in 1991 but the flag dates from June 1992; Wikipedia says the Soviet-era flag remained in use until after December 1991, so the interval is not covered by this flag. The 32-ray sun and ornament details were not compared against a specification.

era-1936.says: Wikipedia: the 1953 flag, red with a hammer and sickle, a star above and a light blue horizontal stripe, was used until after independence in December 1991 (and a 1937 flag with hammer and sickle and the republic's name preceded it). FOTW: the Kazakh SSR flag was 'adopted in 24 January 1953; blue bar in lower part of flag', with construction proportions 6+2+1; Kazakhstan became a Union Republic in 1936.
era-1936.open: The drawing shows the 1953 flag; the 1936-1953 flags (1937 and 1940 variants) are described only by Wikipedia, without detail. FOTW calls the bar blue, Wikipedia light blue.

era-1920.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Kazakhstan): the Kazakh ASSR's first flag had two lines of yellow text (KSSR and R.F.) in the canton inside a yellow border. Wikipedia (Kazakh ASSR): created as the Kirghiz ASSR on 26 August 1920 within the RSFSR, renamed Kazak ASSR in June 1925, union republic 5 December 1936; the article shows a flag image and does not describe the RSFSR flag. FOTW (national page) says the Kirghiz ASSR was renamed Kazakh in 1924 and became a Union Republic in 1936; its Kazakh SSR page gives no 1920-1936 flags.
era-1920.open: The sources contradict this page's claim that the RSFSR flag simply flew; FOTW's 'early flags' sub-page was not reachable from the pages read. The renaming year differs (1924 FOTW, 1925 Wikipedia).

era-1731.says: Neither flag source describes the Russian imperial flag in Kazakhstan. Wikipedia (Kazakh Khanate): on 10 October 1731 the Junior Juz khan Abu'l Khayr swore fealty to Anna of Russia, described as nominal vassalage, and the khanate institution was abolished in the Russian Empire in 1822-1824; FOTW: Russian protection of the Lesser Horde acknowledged 1734, colonial status regulated 1868.
era-1731.open: The Russian imperial tricolour over the steppe is not stated by any source read; 1731 was nominal vassalage and Russian administration was gradual, so the era's start date is not a flag event.

era-1465.says: Wikipedia (Kazakh Khanate): the khanate existed from c. 1465 (Kazakh historiography) to the early 19th century; the infobox shows the tamga of the Tore dynasty; no flag is described. FOTW (Kazakh khanate page): shows an 'ancient flag' dated 1456-1822 but contributors question its authenticity ('suspiciously modern') and whether a Kazakh state existed.
era-1465.open: No source documents a flag of the Khanate; the tamga motif drawn here is a reconstruction, and the Tore tamga is the only emblem a source names. The date differs (1465 Wikipedia, 1456 FOTW).

era-1895.says: Wikipedia: IBEA Company flag 1888-1895; East Africa Protectorate flag 1895-1921; Colony and Protectorate of Kenya 1921-1963; designs not described. Flags of the World (historical flags of Kenya): Blue Ensign with a red lion on a white disc 1895-1921 and with the red lion directly on the fly 1921-1963; the Union Jack with the lion on a white disc and garland 1895-1963; the badge a red lion rampant guardant; British East Africa page: a crown and rayed sun badge for the IBEA Company, and by independence a Blue Ensign with a red lion on a white disc (Stilling).
era-1895.open: Neither source mentions Mount Kenya in the badge; the lion badge dates differ between FOTW's two pages (disc on the fly until 1921 or at independence), and the card's simplified badge is not either form exactly.

era-1800.says: Wikipedia's earliest Kenyan flag is the IBEA Company's, 1888. Flags of the World (British East Africa): the first British flag in what became Kenya was a red Arab flag based on Zanzibar's design with a small Union Jack in the centre, agreed in 1893 at Witu; (Zanzibar) the standard, ensign and merchant flags of Zanzibar are plain red in 1959 and 1918 sources. Neither FOTW page mentions Zanzibar's flag on the Kenyan coast before 1888.
era-1800.open: The plain red banner for c.1800-1895 is consistent with the 1893 Witu flag but no source dates a Zanzibari flag at coastal posts before then; the interior's flags are not covered.

era-1899.says: Wikipedia: Ottoman flag retained under the 1899 protectorate; a red flag 'We trust in God' raised November 1903; a red flag with 'Kuwait' in Arabic adopted 1914 and used to 1921; Shahada added 1921; falcon's claw 1940. FOTW's history page lists flags for 1899-1909, 1909-1915, 1915-1956 and 1956-61, and quotes Lt Cdr Nunn that on 6 November 1914 the Sheikh's boat flew the Turkish flag until it was changed to white Arabic lettering on red.
era-1899.open: The red flag with 'Kuwait' in Arabic is supported only from about 1914 (to 1921 in Wikipedia); the 1899-1914 flag and the post-1921 additions differ, so the single drawing does not fit the whole era.

era-1752.says: Wikipedia: the Sulaimi flag (red with a serrated white ribbon near the mast) raised under Sheikh Sabah I, 1752 in the text and 1746 in the infobox, until 1871, with the Ottoman flag 1871-1914. FOTW's history page says only that before 1899 the flag is 'supposed to have been a plain red flag' (Jaume Olle, 1997).
era-1752.open: The two sources conflict: Wikipedia has a red flag with a white serrated ribbon, FOTW a supposed plain red; FOTW's statement is a supposition. The drawing's plain red field has support only from that supposition.

era-1991.says: Wikipedia's infobox gives adoption on 3 March 1992 and Flags of the World states 'Flag Adopted 1992-MAR-3', by decision of the Supreme Soviet, as a red flag with a golden sun of 40 rays surrounding a stylised tunduk (the roof of a yurt), the rays standing for the forty tribes or Manas's forty soldiers.
era-1991.open: Both sources say the flag was modified on 22 December 2023 (the sun and tunduk redrawn), so the design described here is the 1992-2023 flag; the page's 1991 start precedes the 1992 adoption (FOTW treats 1990-1992 as a Soviet-flag period and calls a flag without the hammer and sickle 'erroneous'). The tunduk's colour (red) is not stated by the sources.

era-1924.says: FOTW: Kara-Kirghiz AO 1924, ASSR 1926, SSR 1936; its early-flags page says no Kyrgyz flags existed in 1926-1936 (a 1929 draft-constitution flag is of unknown use), the 1937 and 1940s flags were red with the name in letters at the hoist, and its SSR page gives a 1952 flag with blue-white-blue stripes (a third of the height, the white 1/20) from the 1978 constitution. Wikipedia: a possible ASSR flag 1929-36, an SSR flag 1936-40 with a bilingual name, and a 1952-91 flag red with star, hammer and sickle and two navy blue bars with a white stripe.
era-1924.open: The two publishers agree on the sequence, but only the 1952-1991 flag matches this page's caption of a hammer and sickle with a stripe, and both give blue bars (Wikipedia: navy) not 'light-blue'; no flag is documented for 1924-1936 or described with a hammer and sickle for 1937-1952. The row's single drawing therefore covers one sub-period of 1924-1991.

era-1876.says: Neither Wikipedia's nor FOTW's Kyrgyzstan page covers Russian Turkestan flags; Wikipedia mentions white rebel banners (1898, 1916) and Shabdan Dzhantayev's white-and-red banner (1916). FOTW's Russian Empire page and Wikipedia's Flag of Russia show that the white-blue-red tricolour was the civil flag, that a black-orange-white (black-yellow-white) flag was the state flag from 1858, that the tricolour was authorised on land in 1883 and made the national flag in 1896. FOTW's Central Asia page gives Turkestan flags of 1917-1924 (Kokand, Basmachi, the Soviet Republic of Turkestan).
era-1876.open: No source read says which flag was flown in Russian Turkestan or that the tricolour was flown 'across' it from 1876; for 1876-1883 the state flag was the black-orange-white one. The Soviet red flag with hammer and sickle for the Turkestan ASSR is not described in the pages read.

era-1876-1.says: Neither Wikipedia's nor FOTW's Kyrgyzstan page nor FOTW's Central Asian Khanates page describes pre-Russian Kyrgyz flags; Wikipedia only links to the Kyrgyz Khaganate and other states.
era-1876-1.open: No source read documents a flag or tribal emblem for the Yenisei Kyrgyz or the Tian Shan confederations; the tribal-emblem motif is the page's own reconstruction.

era-1975.says: Wikipedia: red-blue-red with white disc re-adopted 2 December 1975; designed by Maha Sila Viravong for the Lao Issara (1945); used by Pathet Lao; blue band double the height of each red band. FOTW: the Pathet Lao flag was adopted in 1975 and replaced the flag used since 1952; red blood, blue Mekong/wealth, white full moon and unity.
era-1975.open: Meanings vary between the two sources; whether the Lao Issara ever officially adopted the design is unclear in FOTW.

era-1953.says: Wikipedia: red flag with a white three-headed elephant under a nine-fold umbrella on a five-tier pedestal, used 1952-1975 (caption says 1947-1975), adopted by the Luang Prabang monarchy early in the 20th century. FOTW: the 1952-1975 flag originated as the flag of the Kingdom of Luang Phabang.
era-1953.open: Start date 1952 (not 1953); Lan Xang origin not covered by either source.

era-1893.says: Flags of the World (Laos under the French protectorate): 'the flag of one of the three kingdoms of the zone (Luang Prabang) was adopted, with the French tricolor in the canton' (Jaume Olle, 1996); another contributor says Laos 'had the Tricolore in its flag when it was a French protectorate'; French rule began in 1893; the page does not know whether Vientiane and Champasak had their own flags. Wikipedia: under French rule Luang Prabang's monarchy adopted a red flag with a single white elephant, inspired by a similar Thai flag; its protectorate flag is listed for 1893-1947.
era-1893.open: Both publishers contradict a plain French tricolour as the protectorate's flag; they point instead to the Luang Prabang elephant flag with a tricolour canton, but neither gives the date the canton or elephant flag was adopted or a decree, and Wikipedia's text puts the elephant flag within 1893-1947 without a year.

era-1707.says: Wikipedia lists flags for Vientiane (1707-1828), Luang Phrabang (1707-1893) and Champasak (1713-1904 or 1713-1947) without describing them in text, and says the Luang Prabang monarchy adopted a red flag with a single white elephant, inspired by a Thai flag, under French rule. Flags of the World: the Kingdom of Laos' three-headed elephant flag (1952-1975) 'was originally the flag of the Kingdom of Luang Phabang' (Wilson) and the story of its three heads standing for the three kingdoms 'was made up much later'; its Vientiane page and French-protectorate page describe no flag for the kingdoms, and Olle says he does not know whether Vientiane and Champasak had flags.
era-1707.open: No source read puts an elephant banner on Luang Prabang before the 20th century or describes the 1707-1893 flags Wikipedia lists; the card's elephant flag is the later Luang Prabang or royal design.

FOTW: flag and arms adopted 27 February 1990; independence declaration 4 May 1990; the 1921–39 flag was revived in the 1990 demonstrations.
