era-57bce.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-gojoseon.says: This page's own caption calls the image a placeholder: «placeholder field — earliest Korean state on record, no flag survives».
era-gojoseon.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1945.says: Wikipedia: the flag was widely used again after liberation and the US Army Military Government used it with the US flag from January 1946. FOTW's history page: on 15 August 1945 Japan surrendered and a South Korean Military Administration was set up by US troops; 'the same flag as the present national flag except for the shape of two kwaes' was used in South Korea.
era-1945.open: Neither source calls the flag's use 'informal'; the page's 'flown informally' wording is its own. FOTW does not give the military administration's end date or the 1948 Republic's adoption in this section beyond the general history.

era-1910.says: FOTW's history page: the Hinomaru was used in Korea from the 22 August 1910 annexation until 15 August 1945, after the Resident General's light-blue flag with a Hinomaru canton (adopted 14 February 1906) was abolished; a contributor adds that the t'aeguk flag was prohibited under Japanese rule and was used as a symbol by independence movements (Banzai movement 1919, Independent Army in the 1920s). Wikipedia: a similar flag was used by the government-in-exile in China, 1919-1942.
era-1910.open: The colonial ban on the Taegukgi rests on one FOTW contributor note without a named source; Wikipedia does not mention it. FOTW's text on the Governor-General's flag is also a contributor note (a blue ensign with a Hinomaru canton).

era-1883.says: Wikipedia: no flag in 1876; Shufeldt urged one in 1882; the Taegukgi was promulgated 27 January 1883. FOTW's history page: Pak Yeong-hyo drew a four-trigram flag aboard ship in September 1882 and King Gojong formally proclaimed it on 6 March 1883 (Korea.net), while another contributor note gives 27 January 1883 as the official adoption; a 1882 US Navy chart and a November 1882 copy in the UK National Archives show the four-trigram design.
era-1883.open: The two sources differ on who designed the flag (Wikipedia: Lee Eung-jun, with Pak Yeong-hyo presenting a model; FOTW: Pak Yeong-hyo, with the Chinese delegate Ma Jianzhong pressing the yin-yang design per a Korea Herald report) and on the proclamation date (27 January vs 6 March 1883). Four trigrams are shown in 1882 sources; the 1893 Herold plate with eight trigrams is a disputed contributor report.

era-1897.says: Wikipedia captions a Korean Empire flag (1897-1910) and says the Taegukgi's predecessors were used by the empire. FOTW's history page shows the Denny Taegeukgi (given by Gojong to the American adviser Owen Denny, taken to the US in 1890, returned 1981 and registered as cultural heritage 2008), a 1899 US Navy chart flag 'which might be' the Korean Empire's national flag, and a 1911 geography showing the old flag before 1905 with four trigrams around a yin-yang disc.
era-1897.open: FOTW's 1899 chart identification is hedged ('might be'), and contributors disagree on the trigram colours and arrangement shown in 1890s sources; neither source describes the imperial standards or the empire's status relative to China.

era-1392.says: Wikipedia: no national flag before 1876, a royal standard (gallery caption 1392-1907, design not described) and an undated naval ensign based on the jwadogi. FOTW's history page cites Japanese flag charts: a yellow flag with a black Chinese-style dragon titled 'Korean National flag' (charts of 1856 and 1871) and a blue flag with a yellow dragon titled 'Korean King Standard' (chart of 1876); the Korea Herald account says Korea had little interest in a national symbol before 1875.
era-1392.open: The dragon flags come from Japanese charts of the 1850s-1870s, not Joseon sources, and conflict with each other (yellow vs blue ground), so the royal standard's design in 1392-1883 is unestablished; the blue shown here is a reference colour. No source dates a royal standard back to 1392.

era-918.says: Wikipedia's only Goryeo mention is a caption on an 1883 Qing book showing a 'flag of Goryeo' (Joseon being sometimes called Goryeo in China). FOTW's history page (the Korea section from 1856) and main page do not cover Goryeo.
era-918.open: No source read describes a Goryeo flag or states there was none; a Korean museum or academic source on Goryeo military banners was not found in the pages read.

era-676.says: Neither Wikipedia's flag article nor FOTW's main and history pages mention Silla flags.
era-676.open: No source read covers Silla flags; the statement that Buddhist iconography substitutes for a flag is not supported by any source read.

era-2011.says: Wikipedia: the flag was adopted 9 July 2005 after the Comprehensive Peace Agreement and became the national flag on 9 July 2011 at independence (standardised 25 August 2023); the government's meanings are black the people, red blood shed, green land and agricultural wealth, white peace, blue the Nile, yellow unity of the states, hope and determination; a different version had been the SPLM flag. FOTW: three equal bands of black, red and green, the red edged in white, with a blue hoist triangle holding a yellow five-pointed star; the Transitional Constitution of 6 July 2005 gave the South its own flag; the cabinet approved the flag, the SPLM flag of 2005 used as interim flag by the Government of Southern Sudan, on 22 March 2011 and it became the national flag on 9 July 2011.
era-2011.open: The sources agree on design and on 9 July 2011 as national flag status. They differ on whether the 2005 adoption was Wikipedia's 9 July or FOTW's 6 July constitution date, on whether the 2005 flag was the SPLM flag exactly, and on the meaning of the star (optimism per FOTW, unity per the government).

era-1821-1.says: This page's own caption calls the image a placeholder: «placeholder maroon field — stateless Nilotic peoples, no flag survives».
era-1821-1.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1956.says: WP captions: 1956-1970 Sudan flag used in South Sudan, then the 1970-2011 flag; SPLM/SPLA flag variants from 1983 and 1995. Nile Republic flag 1969-71 caption. FOTW (sd.html): the national flag was adopted 20 May 1970, three horizontal stripes of red, white and black with a green triangle at the hoist, the black stripe said to represent the Mahdiya; the page describes the 1956 emblem (a rhinoceros between palms) but not a 1956-70 flag.
era-1956.open: Wikipedia's captions are the only evidence that Sudan's flags were used in the south and they give no colours; FOTW dates and describes only the 1970 flag. Who controlled the south and the two civil wars are not covered.

era-1899.says: Wikipedia (Anglo-Egyptian Sudan): the condominium was agreed in 1899 (infobox 19 June 1899) and lasted to 1956; the infobox caption reads 'Flags of the United Kingdom and the Kingdom of Egypt respectively', with a governor-general flag and the April 1955 provisional flag also shown; no southern flag is mentioned. Wikipedia (Flag of South Sudan): Anglo-Egyptian Sudan flags 1914-1922 and 1922-1955 shown, undescribed.
era-1899.open: The sources show the British and Egyptian flags as the condominium's symbols but do not say the Union Flag was dominant or how they were flown together; FOTW is silent. The 1899 start is from Wikipedia only.

era-1821.says: Wikipedia (Mahdist State): 1885-1899; the infobox flag is a Mahdist flag (red with blue and salmon rectangles and black Arabic) with the caption that most Mahdist flags varied in colour but were similar in style, and the text says they were usually white with coloured borders and four lines of Arabic; the Ansar began to move into the southern region by the end of 1885. Neither Wikipedia nor FOTW's South Sudan page covers the Ottoman-Egyptian (from c.1821) period.
era-1821.open: No flag specific to the south is described for either regime, and no source covers the Ottoman-Egyptian period; Mahdist flags are described generally. Wikipedia Mahdist text read to 100,000 characters.

era-1975.says: Wikipedia says an eagle change took effect on 21 January 1977, that Article 4.1 of the 1978 Constitution reads «The flag of Spain consists of three horizontal stripes: red, yellow and red», that Royal Decree 441/1981 of 27 February set the colours, and that the current arms date from 1981 (19 December in its text, 5 October in its infobox). FOTW says the Constitution was approved by Congress on 31 October 1978 and ratified on 6 December 1978, that Law 39 of 28 October 1981 allowed the arms on the yellow stripe, and that Royal Decree 2964/1981 (18 December, published 19 December) set the official arms and the flag's construction.
era-1975.open: The sources disagree on the 1981 arms date and on the act number. This page's «flown since 1785» is the naval ensign; the 1843 decree made it the national flag.

era-722.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-218bce.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1939.says: Wikipedia says National Defence Junta Decree No. 77 of 29 August 1936 re-established the red and gold bicolour, that the Eagle of Saint John was added to the shield in 1938, that regulations of 26 July and 11 October 1945 fixed a bicolour with a new eagle in force until 1977. FOTW says a decree of 27 July 1938 set the State and war flag (it does not describe the design).

era-1936.says: La Moncloa (Spanish government): after the uprising rebel troops used many flags, and a decree of 29 August 1936 signed by General Cabanellas stated 'The red and weld bi-colour flag is re-established as the Flag of Spain'. Wikipedia: Decree No. 77 of 29 August 1936 of the National Defence Junta did so and the Eagle of Saint John was added in 1938. Flags of the World: the Republic's tricolour was abolished in parts of the territory on 29 August 1936 and abandoned on 1 April 1939; a decree of 2 February 1938 set the arms with the eagle of St John, and a state flag with the arms in the yellow stripe is shown for about 1938-1977.
era-1936.open: Wikipedia's 1931 article says a military version of the Republic's flag served Republican Army units during the war. La Moncloa dates the restoration to 29 August 1936, not 'immediately' after the July uprising.

era-1931.says: La Moncloa quotes the decree of 27 April 1931: three horizontal strips of equal width, 'the upper being red, the central being yellow and the lower being dark purple'. Flags of the World: decree of 27 April 1931, equal horizontal stripes red-yellow-purple, arms with a mural crown on the central yellow stripe; Wikipedia's Second Republic flag article: the same bands (red, yellow, dark purple), adopted by decree of 27 April 1931, with the arms ensigned by a mural crown between the Pillars of Hercules; purple said to recall Castile's Pendon Morado, which modern historians doubt.
era-1931.open: The page's drawing puts purple on the top and red on the bottom, the reverse of the decree, and the page text gives 14 April (the Republic's proclamation) rather than 27 April 1931 as the flag's date. The Comuneros explanation of the purple is given by Flags of the World as a republican belief and by Wikipedia as an error, so it is not established.

era-1873.says: Wikipedia: the First Republic did not alter the flag's colours but all royal symbols of the monarchy were removed from the coat of arms (flag caption 1873-1874). La Moncloa: plans were drawn up to replace the lower red stripe with purple, but no change was made; the Republic's changes concerned the coat of arms (the mural crown, removal of the Savoy arms).
era-1873.open: Two sources, Wikipedia and a government page, so the colours are corroborated; neither describes the flag's arms beyond the removal of royal symbols. The page's wording that the flag itself lost 'the royal crown' is the arms, not the stripes.

era-1814.says: Wikipedia says a decree of 13 October 1843 from the government of Joaquín María López required Army, Navy and National Militia flags to use the war flag's colours, so that it was adopted by all the Armed Forces. FOTW says a Royal Decree of the same date made it the State and war flag and ensign.
era-1814.open: This page says the decree was under Isabella II, which is the reign; the sources attribute it to the government of the day. The era's claim about the Sexennium arms was not checked.

era-1808.says: Flags of the World: Joseph Bonaparte's flag is a reconstruction, white, with a shield in six quarters (Castile, Leon, Aragon, Navarre, Granada, the Indies) and the imperial eagle at the centre, arms set by Royal Decree of 12 July 1808; the Lyon library says it is not certain it was much used by Spaniards. La Moncloa: Joseph's arms had six quarterings and an inescutcheon with the Bonaparte arms (given in its coat-of-arms section, not as a flag). Wikipedia: the red-weld was used by the people from 1808; it does not mention Joseph.
era-1808.open: The page shows a red-yellow-red bicolour with an eagle, which neither FOTW (white field) nor La Moncloa supports; whether Joseph's flag was white is itself a reconstruction. The Spanish national and naval use of the bicolour in 1808-1814 is not covered by FOTW's page.

era-1716.says: Wikipedia says a royal decree of 28 May 1785 set a red-yellow-red flag with a double-width yellow centre, to avoid confusion with other nations' flags «at long distances or with calm winds». FOTW says twelve war-ensign proposals were designed at the king's request and that a Royal Decree of 25 May 1785 set the war ensign.
era-1716.open: The decree date differs by three days (28 or 25 May 1785).

era-1516.says: Flags of the World: the red Burgundy saltire on a usually white field was the Spanish ensign 1506 to the 1670s and then a jack to 1785, brought in as the personal badge of Philip the Handsome, used first by the Tercios and the Spanish military flag from the 16th century to 1843; fields varied. Wikipedia: from the reign of Charles I (1516-1556) Spanish armies used flags with the Cross of Burgundy on different fields, and Philip II is said (citation needed) to have ordered a yellow flag with the red cross for each Tercio.
era-1516.open: The field was not always white (yellow, blue and purple are reported); FOTW ties the emblem to Philip the Handsome, whereas the page says it came from Charles's grandmother Mary of Burgundy (not stated in either source). Era dates 1516-1716 do not match the sources' 1506-1785/1843.

era-1874.says: Wikipedia: the national flag is listed as used 1874-1931 without a crown wording, and a crowned yacht ensign was established by royal decree in 1875 with the crown on the central stripe. Flags of the World (main page) lists a state and war flag and ensign by Royal Decree of 13 October 1843 and says nothing on the arms or a crown for 1843-1931. La Moncloa quotes the 1843 decree (all flags replaced by new red-weld ones) and has no 1874 entry.
era-1874.open: No source read states whether the Restoration flag carried crowned arms; the 1875 crown is stated only for the yacht ensign. Not found: a Restoration-period regulation of the national flag's arms.

era-1479.says: Flags of the World: the Catholic Kings' royal standard (1492-1506) was white with the joint arms, Castile and Leon counterquartered in the first and fourth quarters and Aragon and Sicily per pale in the second and third, with a pomegranate for Granada added after 1492; the realms stayed distinct (Isabella queen of Castile and Leon, Ferdinand king of Aragon and Sicily) and the earlier ensigns were used until 1517. Wikipedia: a Catholic Monarchs' pennant dated 1475-1492; the Castilian and Aragonese flags and arms merged for the 1475 union [citation needed]; Crown of Aragon flag yellow with four red stripes.
era-1479.open: The two sources agree on a combined arms of the two crowns but not on a date (1475 / 1492-1506) and neither names 1479; FOTW shows the combination in the arms while the realms stay separate, which fits 'side by side' only if the arms themselves are not 'merged'.

era-1230.says: Wikipedia: since the final union of Castile and Leon in 1230 the Crown used a quartered flag alternating the Castilian tower and the Leonese lion. Flags of the World (Castile and Leon): the crowns were definitively united under Ferdinand III in 1230, the quartered castle-and-lion arms were devised then, the flag became the Castilian navy ensign in 1248 and was used until 1516; the 14th-century Book of All Kingdoms describes a pendon with two castles and two lions.
era-1230.open: The sources differ on the early castle form (embattled wall with towers, not the later castle) and FOTW's own page is inconsistent on the end date (early 15th century vs 1516); the first banner in this exact quartered form is later than 1230.

era-1972.says: Wikipedia's infobox gives the adoption as 22 May 1972. Flags of the World's history page says the amended flag, with the stylised corner leaves redrawn as natural bo leaves, was first unfurled at the Republic Day celebrations on 22 May 1972, and that the flag is incorporated in the Second Schedule of the constitution of 9 September 1978; the main FOTW page's 1978 is that constitution date.
era-1972.open: The two FOTW pages differ on the year (1978 on the main page, 1972 on the history page); 1972 is given by Wikipedia and the history page. Only the date and the bo-leaf change were compared; the colours were not checked against a specification, and a further small change to the leaves and background shade in 1978 is mentioned by FOTW contributors.

era-1948.says: Wikipedia: 16 Jan 1948 motion by A. Sinnalebbe to make the Lion Flag national; flag adopted for the Dominion; its gallery dates a version 1951-1972 while its text says changes in 1953 and 1972. FOTW: Lion Flag flew at independence 4 Feb 1948; a committee chaired by S.W.R.D. Bandaranaike designed a gold lion on dark red with yellow border; two stripes (green, yellow/orange, each 1/7) added when Parliament adopted the flag on 2 March 1951 to represent Muslims and Tamils.
era-1948.open: 1951 vs 1953 date conflict inside Wikipedia; FOTW and Wikipedia differ on the 1948 corner motifs.

era-1796.says: Wikipedia: the Union Flag replaced the Kandyan royal standard in 1815; colonial flags are shown for 1815-1875 and 1875-1948 without design description. FOTW (British Ceylon page, quoting David Prothero): the colonial badge, a brown elephant before a dagoba on dark blue in a red ring, was used in the fly of the Blue Ensign of government vessels from c.1875 to 1948 and on the governor's Union Jack.
era-1796.open: The blue ensign with the colonial badge is established only for c.1875-1948; nothing read gives the flag for 1796-1875, and 1796 is not a flag date in either source (1815 is when the Kandyan flag fell). The Blue Ensign appears here as a government ensign; use as the colony's general flag was not read.

era-1658.says: Wikipedia (Dutch Ceylon) calls the territory a governorate of the Dutch East India Company and its infobox shows the company flag, a tricolour with the VOC monogram. Flags of the World (VOC page) is a contributor discussion; one contributor says the VOC monogram was rarely used abroad on the 17th-century paintings he saw, and another quotes Brownell that the flag flown was either the Netherlands flag or the company's version of it with the cypher.
era-1658.open: No source says which of the two flags was flown in Ceylon, or from 1658 to 1796 specifically; the page's claim that the monogram flag marked company rather than state territory is not stated. The VOC flag shown here as the era's flag rests on a Wikipedia infobox image.

era-1505.says: Neither Wikipedia nor FOTW's Sri Lanka pages describe a Portuguese flag for Ceylon. Flags of the World's Portugal pages say the red cross of the Order of Christ was used on the Discovery ships as flag and on sails, over white, green or gyronny backgrounds.
era-1505.open: A Portuguese flag specific to Ceylon, and the claim that none existed, are not covered. The Order of Christ flag is shown for Portuguese ships in general; use on forts in Ceylon was not read. Wikipedia's Portuguese Ceylon infobox shows the 1640 Portuguese flag, not an Order of Christ flag.

era-1592.says: Wikipedia: the standard of Sri Vikrama Rajasinha served as the Kandy kingdom's flag (c.1798-1815) and the lion design was used until 1815. Wikipedia's Flags of the Kingdom of Kandy, citing E. W. Perera (1916) and a Malwatte manuscript, describes the flag of Sri Vikrama Rajasinha (1798-1815) as a lion holding a sword, rediscovered at the Royal Hospital Chelsea in 1908, and shows an earlier royal standard of 1785. FOTW (history page, quoting DK Pocket Book 1997): the lion flag was used as the national flag of Ceylon before 1815, with temple finials, not bo leaves, in the corners.
era-1592.open: The sources give the lion flag only from 1785 to 1815; no source read gives a Kandyan flag for 1592-1785. The 'unchanged to 1948' descent is not stated: Wikipedia says the Royal Standard basis of the modern flag was modified, and FOTW dates stripes to 1951.

era-1236.says: Wikipedia shows flags for Gampola (c. 1341-1408), Kotte (c. 1412-1597) and Sitawaka (c. 1521-1594) without describing them. FOTW: some older Kotte-era flags showed a whip instead of a sword, undated.
era-1236.open: Dambadeniya not covered; no source states a settled lion-and-sword emblem for the period.

era-1070.says: Neither Wikipedia's Flag of Sri Lanka nor FOTW's Sri Lanka pages describe a Polonnaruwa-period flag. Wikipedia's Kingdom of Polonnaruwa article, searched for flag, banner, standard and lion, has no flag in its infobox and no text on one. FOTW's history page (lk_his) mentions a lion on 'older Kotte era flags' with a whip in place of the sword, which is a later kingdom.
era-1070.open: Lion emblem continuity from Anuradhapura to Polonnaruwa is not covered by any source read; the silence of Wikipedia's kingdom article is not evidence of no flag.

era-993.says: Neither Wikipedia nor FOTW's Sri Lanka pages mention a Chola flag in Ceylon. Wikipedia's Chola dynasty article shows an Uttama Chola silver coin found in Sri Lanka bearing the dynasty's tiger emblem.
era-993.open: The tiger is attested as a Chola emblem on a coin found in Sri Lanka, but a Chola banner for Ceylon, or a tiger on a gold field, is not described. The Polonnaruwa row (era-1070) found nothing new in Wikipedia's kingdom article or on FOTW.

era-377bce.says: Wikipedia: a Dambulla Cave no. 2 mural shows Dutugemunu (c. 162 BC) under a banner with a lion holding a sword, the only ancient representation of the lion flag (lion defaced in 1957); lion linked to Prince Vijaya in the Mahavamsa. FOTW does not cover this period.
era-377bce.open: Dating of the mural and any flag for 377 BCE-993 CE needs an archaeological source; FOTW silent.

era-1970.says: Both sources give 1970, the year this page starts the current flag. Wikipedia's infobox gives the adoption as 20 May 1970; Flags of the World dates it 20 May 1970.
era-1970.open: Only the year the current flag was adopted was compared; the design and the swatch colours were not checked against a specification.

era-1504.says: This page's own caption calls the image a placeholder: «placeholder maroon field — the Funj Sultanate».
era-1504.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1070.says: This page's own caption calls the image a placeholder: «placeholder maroon field — Kush and medieval Christian Nubia».
era-1070.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-2500bce.says: This page's own caption calls the image a placeholder: «placeholder maroon field — Kingdom of Kerma, no flag survives».
era-2500bce.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1956.says: Wikipedia: flag adopted 1 January 1956, designed by Macki Sufi; blue for the Nile, yellow for the Sahara, green for farmlands; used until 1970 and again in the 2018-19 protests. Flags of the World (historical flags, Ollé 1996): 'First flag of independent Sudan was a blue over yellow over green tricolour', adopted 1 January 1956 and used since 1954, in use until 1970 (Stilling 1996); a naval ensign was white with the national flag in the canton. Flags of the World's main page describes only the 1956 emblem (a rhinoceros), and does not mention Macki Sufi.
era-1956.open: Macki Sufi and the meanings of the colours rest on Wikipedia alone; the page's earlier meanings (peace, the south) are in neither source; Flags of the World's 'used since 1954' is not matched by Wikipedia.

era-1899.says: Wikipedia (Anglo-Egyptian Sudan): infobox shows the Union Jack and the Egyptian flag (1922-1958) captioned 'Flags of the United Kingdom and the Kingdom of Egypt', 1899-1956; Wikipedia's flag article adds that the British flag took precedence. Flags of the World (historical flags): no individual flag, 'the two flags of Egypt and the United Kingdom were used, with the British flag taking precedence' (Smith 1975: Union Jack always first, except at Suakin where only the Egyptian flag flew); the Governor-General's flag was a Union Jack with a white disc and laurel garland (Prothero 1999); a white 'SUDAN' flag was made for the April 1955 Bandung conference; a so-called Anglo-Egyptian Sudan flag is called 'completely fictitious' (Kelly 2022).
era-1899.open: The Egyptian flag changed in this period (red with crescent and star until 1914; three crescents and stars 1914-1923; green with crescent and three stars 1923-1954 per Heimer citing Smith) and the page does not say which one it draws.

era-1885.says: Wikipedia (Mahdist State): the state 'had no uniform flags'; most flags carried four lines of Arabic text for God, Muhammad and the Mahdi and were usually white with coloured borders; units were called raya after their standards, with a 'Black Flag' of Baggara recruits; infobox caption 'one of the flags of the Mahdi movement', dated 1885-1899. Flags of the World (historical flags): a black-red-green tricolour with a white crescent and spear (Sensen 1996), a green-gold-green silk strip banner with white lettering in the 1880s (Garrison 2023), and the 'black banner of the Khalifa's brother' with 'blue and white banners of his son' at Omdurman (Mills citing Stevens).
era-1885.open: Two publishers agree that Mahdist flags were varied and inscribed with Arabic text, but neither describes a single black banner as the state's flag, so this page's caption is not confirmed; Wikipedia's Omdurman account mentions no flags.

era-1821.says: Wikipedia (Ottoman Egypt) dates Muhammad Ali's conquest of Sudan to 1820-1822 and its infobox shows the 'Flag of Eyalet of Egypt' (design not described in text); Wikipedia (Khedivate of Egypt) says Muhammad Ali expanded control to Sudan and describes no flag for Sudan. Flags of the World (historical flags): 'no information on flags from this period' (1821-1885); it does give the Egyptian flag as red with a crescent and star until 1914.
era-1821.open: No source read describes a flag used in Sudan under Turco-Egyptian rule; the Egyptian flag with a crescent and star is inferred from Egypt's own flag history, not stated for Sudan.

era-1975.says: Wikipedia: five horizontal bands of green, white, red (quadruple width), white and green with a large yellow five-pointed star, designed in a national competition (winner Jack Pinas) and accepted by parliament in 1975; red represents progress, white freedom and justice, green the fertility of the land, the star unity and a golden future. FOTW: the flag was established by a decree of the Governor dated 25 November 1975, published in the Government Gazette of 24 November 1975, with the colours defined and the same meanings (red progress and love, green hope and fertility, white peace and justice, the star unity of all ethnic groups).
era-1975.open: The sources give the symbolism differently from the page, which says red stands for 'justice and the road to independence'; Wikipedia gives red as progress and white as freedom and justice. FOTW also reports a 'new national flag?' discussion, but no change since 1975.

era-1500.says: This page's own caption calls the image a placeholder: «placeholder maroon field — indigenous and earliest colonial era, no flag survives».
era-1500.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1954.says: Wikipedia: the pre-independence flag, designed by Noni Lichtveld and adopted in 1959 after the Charter for the Kingdom, was a plain white field with five coloured stars (black for Africans, brown for Asian Indians, yellow for Javanese and Chinese, red for Amerindians, white for Europeans) connected by a black ellipse; it was also the governor's flag and was replaced in 1975. FOTW: the National Decree of 8 December 1959 (effective 15 December 1959) defines a white field with five black-bordered stars in black, brown, yellow, red and white linked by an elliptical black band; the flag of the overseas territory was abolished on 25 November 1975.
era-1954.open: The page's red oval is contradicted: both sources give a black ellipse. The flag dates from 1959, not 1954 (the year of the Charter), and FOTW's own headings also give 1966 for the territory flag; FOTW names Frank Essed as designer where Wikipedia names Noni Lichtveld.

era-1667.says: Wikipedia: after the Kingdom of the Netherlands was established in 1815 the Dutch tricolour was used in the colony; a colony flag with the arms was discussed but not used; the governor's flag before 1959 was the Dutch flag with white circles in the top-left corner. FOTW: the Treaty of Breda gave Suriname to the Dutch in 1667; a flag with the three-master arms exists in a doubtful source, but a contributor finds that photographs (1870-1955) and detailed drawings of Fort Zeelandia (16xx-1900) show a tricolour without arms, concluding the arms flag was never used in the colony.
era-1667.open: Wikipedia covers 1815-1959 only; for 1667-1815 the only support is one FOTW contributor's reading of drawings, and the sources do not describe the flags of the West India Company or the Society of Suriname. The Dutch flag's colours before the 19th century are not covered.

era-1905.says: Wikipedia: a law of 28 October 1905 removed the union mark from the Swedish flag as of 1 November 1905, and the flag law of 22 June 1906 set the colours as light medium blue and gold-yellow. Store norske leksikon (Roede): the union mark was removed from Swedish flags on 1 November 1905 after the dissolution of the union; the flag law of 22 June 1906 changed the blue to the lighter 'ljust mellanblå' (the earlier blue was dark, much like Norway's); the national, merchant and state flag adopted 22 June 1906 in proportions 5:8. FOTW: flag 'officially re-adopted 22 June 1906', with pictures of a blue cloth with a yellow cross from the 16th century.
era-1905.open: The flag was not 'unchanged since 1905': the blue was lightened in 1906; 'longest unbroken run of any flag in this lineage' is the page's own comparison, not in the sources.

era-900.says: This page's own caption calls the image a placeholder: «placeholder maroon field — pre-unification era, no flag survives».
era-900.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-98.says: This page's own caption calls the image a placeholder: «placeholder maroon field — Suiones & Vendel-era Sweden, no flag survives».
era-98.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1814.says: Wikipedia: a common military ensign for Sweden and Norway with a white saltire on red in the canton was set on 6 June 1815, a common square-cut civil ensign in 1818, and a royal resolution of 20 June 1844 introduced the union mark (the combined colours of both countries) on civil and naval ensigns. Store norske leksikon (Roede): in 1844-1905 the flag carried the union mark ('Sildesalaten') in the upper hoist field, introduced to meet Norwegian demands for equality in the union; it was adopted in both countries as the naval jack and was the common flag of the diplomatic missions abroad.
era-1814.open: Sources describe the union mark as combining Swedish and Norwegian colours (blue, yellow, red, white), not simply 'red-white-blue'; 1814-1844 flags (the 1815 common naval ensign) are given by Wikipedia alone.

era-1523.says: Wikipedia says the oldest recorded pictures of a blue cloth with a yellow cross date from the early 1500s (citation needed), that the first legal description is a royal warrant of 19 April 1562, and that a warrant of 1569 required the yellow cross on battle standards and banners. FOTW, quoting a Swedish Institute leaflet, gives the same early-16th-century pictures, the 1569 warrant, reliable evidence on Swedish vessels from the 1620s under Gustav II Adolf, and the oldest existing flag warrant of 1663 (a triple-tailed flag, merchant ships square-cut).
era-1523.open: Neither source dates the flag to 1523. This page used to say the cross was the settled national banner throughout 1523–1814; the sources give 1562 and 1569 as the first legal steps and the 1620s as reliable evidence at sea. Wikipedia gives 1442 and 1448 for the arms that inspired it, inconsistently.

era-1397.says: FOTW and Wikipedia (Emblems of the Kalmar Union) both cite two letters of 1430 in which King Eric orders the priests of Vadstena and Kalmar to wear the 'banner of the realms', described as a red cross in a yellow field; FOTW adds there is no pictorial evidence or surviving flag and that a red-cross-on-yellow flag in a museum is a recreation. Wikipedia's emblems article puts the Three Crowns (Sweden's older device, which in the 15th century came to represent the three kingdoms) in the union arms, not on the banner.
era-1397.open: No source puts three crowns on the banner, so the page's crowns on a red-and-gold cross field are unconfirmed; the red cross on yellow rests on two 1430 letters only.

era-995.says: Wikipedia says the Three Crowns on blue appear since at least 1336 and that blue and yellow are said to have been Swedish colours since Magnus III's arms in 1275 (no citation).
era-995.open: Arms, not a flag. The page's mention of Magnus Eriksson's seals was not found in the source, and the earliest date given there is 1336, not 995.

era-1848.says: Wikipedia says a federal decree of 12 December 1889 set the cross arms at one-sixth longer than wide (7:6), that the Federal Act on the protection of arms of 2013 (in force 2017) defines the flag as a Swiss cross on a square background, and that the cross height was fixed at 5:8 in 2017. FOTW says Federal Order no. 111 of 12 December 1889 set the cross's relative dimensions with arms one sixth longer than wide, that Act no. 232.21 of 2013 defines the flag and colours, and that the margin was not officially fixed before 2017.
era-1848.open: The sources disagree on 1848: Wikipedia says the Federal Constitution did not name a national flag but prescribed the federal flag for federal troops, while FOTW says the flag was enshrined in the Constitution of 1848. This page says the 1889 decree fixed the proportions «for the first time»; FOTW says it replaced a five-square cross.

era-58bce.says: This page's own caption calls the image a placeholder: «placeholder maroon field — Helvetii, Roman Helvetia, and early medieval overlordship, no flag survives».
era-58bce.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1815.says: Wikipedia says the Tagsatzung reintroduced the white cross on red for the federal seal, accepted on 4 July 1815, and that Bachmann's battalion flag of 12 October 1815 had a red square field and a white cross. FOTW says the restored Confederation adopted a seal with a short white cross and that honorary flags were given to returning regiments in 1815.
era-1815.open: Both sources describe the seal and army flags, not a national flag; Wikipedia says the Constitution of 1848 did not name one.

era-1798.says: Wikipedia: the Helvetic Republic replaced the earlier flags with a green, red and yellow tricolour. FOTW (Helvetic Republic 1798-1803): the flag was green-red-yellow horizontally, the colours being adopted as national colours and cockade colours by the General Assembly on 14 April 1798, with the Directorate fixing details on 13 February 1799; the legion regiments carried flags with William Tell. The cantonal government of Basel-Stadt (1998 press release): green-red-yellow was the national flag of the 'one and indivisible Helvetic Republic'. Universität Freiburg: the French chose a green-red-yellow tricolour rather than a Swiss cross, and it vanished after a few years. The HLS dates the republic 12 April 1798 - 10 March 1803 and shows an 1798 flag in the Bundesbriefmuseum.
era-1798.open: The Liberty figure drawn on the page is not confirmed by any source read; the HLS photograph is of the flag but its stripe order was not read as text.

era-1291.says: Wikipedia says the first attested use of a white cross to identify Confederate troops was at Laupen in 1339, as two textile strips on clothing, and that at Arbedo about 1422 a triangular red flag with an elongated white cross was possibly the first flag used for the Confederacy rather than one canton. FOTW (Mills) says the Laupen troops wore a long-armed white linen cross stitched on breasts, sleeves and thighs, that at Arbedo in 1422 Confederate levies carried red triangular guidons with a white cross, and that the assumption that the flag derives from Schwyz's red banner is incorrect.
era-1291.open: The origin is unproven: FOTW mentions a derivation from a Holy Roman Empire banner, a tenuous Theban Legion link and a stitched-stripes theory. 1291 is the Confederacy's traditional founding, not a flag date.

era-1648.says: Wikipedia: white cross a field sign by the late 13th–early 14th century; Laupen 1339; Arbedo 1422 triangular banner; 1540 first mention of a separate Confederate flag. FOTW: 1339 white linen crosses; 1422 red triangular guidons with a white cross; 1540 last battlefield use; the Confederation was flagless in 1798.
era-1648.open: The 1648 recognition date is not in either source.

era-1803.says: FOTW (Switzerland): the Confederation used no federal flag; the white cross on red disappeared from use after 1540 until the French invasion of 1798; a honorary federal flag was granted to regiments returning from France in 1815 and General Dufour's flag followed in 1821/1833. Wikipedia: Bachmann used the white-on-red cross in 1800 and 1815; the Diet adopted a seal with a white cross on 4 July 1815 and a battalion flag on 12 October 1815. The HLS dates the Helvetic Republic to 10 March 1803, when the Act of Mediation began.
era-1803.open: Neither source describes flags in 1803-1815 (the Mediation) or says whether the old cross persisted at cantonal level; the page's caption is unsupported. Next: cantonal flags of the Mediation cantons (e.g. Staatsarchiv catalogues) and Mattern (1974), cited by FOTW but not read.

era-2024.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Syria, infobox and 'Transitional Period' section): the caretaker government used the green-white-black three-red-star revolution flag de facto from 8 December 2024 and the Constitutional Declaration of 13 March 2025 retained it as the national flag (2:3). Flags of the World (Syria page): the interim constitution adopted on 13 March 2025 defines the flag in its Article 6 as green, white, black with three red stars in the white band. FOTW's 'Historical Flags Since 1932' page lists 1980-2024 for the two-star flag and 'Since 2025' for the reintroduced green-white-black tricolour.
era-2024.open: Only Wikipedia gives 8 December 2024 as the first de facto use; FOTW dates the flag from 2025. Wikipedia's late-2011 date is for first use by the opposition, not the state. Star size and the swatch colours were not checked against a specification.

era-636-1.says: This page's own caption calls the image a placeholder: «placeholder maroon field — pre-heraldic antiquity».
era-636-1.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1958.says: Wikipedia's «Flag of the United Arab Republic» gives adoption in 1958 and relinquishment in 1961, 1972, within a year of this era's 1958 and 1961. The Flags of the World page that article links also carries 1961, and has 1958 next to a word about adopting.
era-1958.open: Only the dates were compared. The Flags of the World page was matched on the two years appearing in its text and on one of them sitting beside the word adopt, introduce, establish or the like; it was not read for what it says about this flag. The design and the swatch colours were not checked against a specification.

era-1980.says: Wikipedia: the 1972 Federation flag was abrogated on 29 March 1980 and replaced by a red-white-black flag with two stars, described as the 1958-61 UAR flag readopted. FOTW 'Historical Flags Since 1932': 1980-2024 was a reintroduction of the United Arab Republic flag of 1958-61, ratio 2:3; the overview page lists it as the red-white-black flag with two green stars, 1980-2024.
era-1980.open: The exact 29 March 1980 date is Wikipedia's alone; FOTW gives only the years. What the flag is called in Syrian law was not found.

era-1961.says: Wikipedia: the green-white-black independence flag with three red stars was restored on 28 September 1961 and replaced on 1 May 1963 by a three-green-star flag and on 1 January 1972 by the Federation of Arab Republics flag. FOTW 'Historical Flags Since 1932': Syria left the union on 28 September 1961 and reverted to the 1946-58 flag; separate entries follow for 1963-1972 (red-white-black, three green stars) and 1972-1980 (Federation flag with the Hawk of Quraish).
era-1961.open: Both sources show the restored flag lasted only to 1963, so the page's 1961-1980 span for this drawing is too long; the later flags are not drawn on this page. FOTW gives 28 September in one note and 29 September in another for the raising.

era-1946.says: Wikipedia: flag defined by decree 3111 of 14 May 1930, ratio 1:2, three red five-pointed stars; adopted for independence on 17 April 1946; replaced by the UAR flag in 1958. FOTW 'Historical Flags Since 1932': green-white-black with three red five-pointed stars, 1:2, for 1946 (independence) to 1958; first hoisted in Aleppo on 1 January 1932 and in Damascus on 11 June 1932. FOTW 'Until 1932' quotes Article 4 of the 14 May 1930 constitution from the League of Nations Official Journal (three equal bands green, white, black, with three red five-pointed stars, length double the height).
era-1946.open: The sources differ on the flag's origin: 14 May 1930 (decree text, Wikipedia) against 1 January and 11 June 1932 (first hoisting, FOTW); FOTW calls a separate 1930-32 flag 'probably erroneous'. The 1946-58 years themselves are stated by FOTW's headings and by Wikipedia.

era-1920.says: Wikipedia: local flags 1920-1930 (Gouraud flag 24 July-1 September 1920; green-white-green Federation of Syria flag with a French canton from 22 June 1922; State of Syria to the 14 May 1930 republic). FOTW 'Until 1932' (extracting Corre 2000 and Ollé): the same Federation flag of 22 June 1922, the State of Syria's green-white-green flag with a French tricolour canton extending over half the flag (1925-30), a sky-blue crescent flag with a French tricolour canton that 'might have been used' in July-August 1920, and the green-white-black three-star flag in the Navy's records from 1930 (the League of Nations text of the 14 May 1930 constitution).
era-1920.open: Neither source shows the plain French tricolour as Syria's flag: it appears only as the canton of the local flags, so the page's drawing is not supported. FOTW marks several of these entries (1924-25 State of Syria, 1930-32 Republic) as probably erroneous and the 1920 sky-blue flag as only possibly used. The page's drawing for 1920-1946 should be replaced; the 1932-1946 autonomy-era flag is the green-white-black one.

era-1517.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Syria): the Ottoman flag was used in Syria until 18 September 1918. FOTW 'Until 1932': before 1918 Syria was part of the Ottoman Empire and used the Ottoman flag. Wikipedia (Mamluk Sultanate), citing the chronicler Ibn Tulun: after Selim I took Damascus in 1516 the yellow Mamluk banner was replaced by a plain red Ottoman banner. Wikipedia (Flag of the Ottoman Empire): the white crescent and star on red came into naval use in 1793 and was made the official flag in 1844; in the 16th and 17th centuries war flags often showed the Zulfiqar sword.
era-1517.open: The dates and the Ottoman identity are attested, but the drawing (red with crescent and star) is documented only for 1793/1844-1918; for 1517 to the late 18th century the sources point to plain red banners or Zulfiqar war flags. Nothing read says how the eyalets of Damascus and Aleppo flew the flag.

era-1260.says: Wikipedia (Mamluk Sultanate): sultans and emirs bore personal blazons shown on their banners (Baybars a panther or lion, Qalawun a fleur-de-lis), and the sultans followed the Ayyubids in using yellow for sultanic banners; the article's infobox flag is deliberately blank. FOTW 'Until 1932': Damascus in the late-14th-century Book of All Kingdoms is a yellow flag with a white crescent. Wikipedia (Zengid dynasty): yellow remained the symbolic colour of the Ayyubid and Mamluk rulers.
era-1260.open: Yellow sultanic banners and personal blazons are attested; no source gives a single state flag, and none gives an eagle blazon for the Mamluks (the eagle belongs to the Saladin tradition), so the page's gold field with an eagle is a reconstruction. The Book of All Kingdoms depicts Damascus as yellow with a white crescent.

era-1174.says: Wikipedia (Zengid dynasty): Saladin's flag was yellow, emblazoned with an eagle, apparently inherited from the Zengids; yellow remained the ruler colour of the Ayyubids and Mamluks. Wikipedia (Mamluk Sultanate): the Mamluk sultans followed the Ayyubids in using yellow for sultanic banners.
era-1174.open: A yellow banner with an eagle is the only Zengid/Ayyubid banner described, and the article calls it 'supposed' and 'apparently inherited'; the page's dark field is not supported by it. No source read gives a Syria-wide state flag for 1174-1260, and no second publisher or reference work was found for Saladin's eagle banner.

era-750.says: Wikipedia (Abbasid Caliphate): the infobox shows the Abbasid Black Standard; the text says the Abbasids kept black as their dynastic colour for banners, headdresses and garments, in contrast to the white of the Umayyads. FOTW 'Pan-Arab Colours' (quoting Abdul Hadi 1986): the Abbasid dynasty (750-1258), ruling from Baghdad, took black as a symbol of mourning for the Prophet's relatives and for Karbala.
era-750.open: Both sources give the colour of the dynasty's banners, not a flag of Syria; neither describes banners of the local successor dynasties between 750 and 1174, which the page rightly does not treat as one flag.

era-636.says: Wikipedia (Umayyad Caliphate): the Umayyad banners were white, after the banner of Mu'awiya ibn Abi Sufyan; the infobox deliberately carries no flag. FOTW 'Pan-Arab Colours' (quoting Abdul Hadi 1986): the Umayyads (661-750, Damascus) took white as their symbolic colour, to recall the Battle of Badr and to set themselves apart from the Abbasids' black.
era-636.open: The sources give a dynastic colour, not a documented design beyond a plain field; they date Umayyad rule from 661 (Mu'awiya), not 636, which is the year of the Muslim conquest of Syria.

era-1949.says: Wikipedia's Flag of the Republic of China says the flag was made the national flag by the Nationalist government in 1928 and, after the defeat in the civil war and the 1949 founding of the PRC, has remained in official use in the Taiwan Area. FOTW's Taiwan page dates the flag to 1928 (Decree No. 47, 19 December 1928) and its Chinese Republic history says the Nationalist government took residence in Taiwan from 1949, retaining the flag.
era-1949.open: Design and swatch colours were not checked against a specification. FOTW's contributors stress that Taiwan had been ROC-ruled since 1945, so 1949 marks the government's retreat, not the flag's arrival.

era-1624-1.says: This page's own caption calls the image a placeholder: «placeholder green field — pre-colonial era, no flag survives».
era-1624-1.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1945.says: Wikipedia's infobox gives 25 October 1945 for adoption in Taiwan (flag law of December 1928 on the mainland). FOTW gives 1928 (Decree No. 47, 19 December 1928) and, in a contributor's comment, says Taiwan has been under ROC rule since 1945.
era-1945.open: 'Ordinary province for the first time' is not covered; FOTW's 1945 support is a contributor comment, not the page text.

era-1895.says: Wikipedia's Taiwan under Japanese rule shows the 1870 Japanese merchant flag as the infobox flag and the Yellow Tiger flag of the 1895 Republic of Formosa as predecessor; FOTW lists Government-General flags of 1898-1945 (ensigns, police, post) and, for the 25 May-7 June 1895 Democratic Republic, a yellow tiger on a blue or black field.
era-1895.open: Neither source's text says the Hinomaru was the flag raised over colonial Taiwan; the page's drawing rests on the infobox image only. The 1895 republic's tiger flag and the Government-General's own flags are not drawn here.

era-1683.says: Wikipedia's Taiwan under Qing rule shows the Qing flag of 1889-1895 as its infobox flag (with a 'Flag' caption for 1889-1895 only) and gives no flag text; FOTW's Imperial Dragon Flag page shows yellow dragon flags of 1872 and 1890 for China without mentioning Taiwan.
era-1683.open: Nothing read says which flag flew in Taiwan 1683-1889, or that the yellow dragon flag was the Taiwan flag before 1889; the page's 1889 formal adoption is not stated by the sources read.

era-1661.says: Wikipedia's Kingdom of Tungning article lists a 'Ming Cheng' flag image against its rulers and mentions a junk flying Koxinga's flag arriving at Fort Zeelandia on 9 July 1656; it describes neither. FOTW's Taiwan pages do not mention Tungning.
era-1661.open: The Ming red-gold reference is not covered; no description of a Tungning flag was found in any page read.

era-1624.says: Wikipedia's Dutch Formosa shows the Dutch East India Company flag as its infobox flag and says village leaders were given a Prince's Flag (Prinsenvlag, the flag of William the Silent) to display; FOTW's Taiwan page does not cover the Dutch period.
era-1624.open: That the Prince's Flag flew over Fort Zeelandia itself is not stated; the infobox gives the VOC flag, so the flag over the fort may have been the VOC's. Spanish Formosa (1626-42) has a Cross of Burgundy infobox flag in Wikipedia, not drawn here.

era-1991.says: Wikipedia: the national flag was adopted on 24 November 1992 (red, white, green in 2:3:2, yellow crown with an arc of seven stars; designer Zuhur Habibullaev), replacing the Tajik SSR flag. FOTW: adopted 24 November 1992 by law; white stripe 1.5 times the width of red and green; independence recognised 9 September 1991; before the new design the former Soviet colours were used without communist symbols (undated).
era-1991.open: The page's era start 1991 is the independence year; the flag itself dates from 1992. 'Unchanged through the civil war' is not covered.

era-8bce.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-bmac.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1929.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Tajikistan): the Tajik SSR flag was approved in 1953, derived from the USSR flag with added white and green stripes, and used until 1992; Wikipedia (Tajik SSR) dates the infobox flag 1953-1991. FOTW (su-tj): adopted 20 March 1953, red with white and green stripes near the bottom, hammer and sickle with star on the obverse. FOTW (tj-ir, reproducing Encyclopaedia Iranica): the Tajik ASSR constitution of 28 April 1929 set a red flag (1:2) with the state arms upper left; February 1931 a plain red flag with a Russian inscription in gold letters; 20 March 1953 the red flag with white and green stripes.
era-1929.open: Attested for the Soviet red flag, the 1929 and 1931 forms and the 1953-91 stripes design. The gold stripe drawn on the page is not in any source. FOTW's Iranica-based text is a copy; the Iranica site itself returned 403 and was not read. The republic's status (ASSR to 1929, SSR from 5 December 1929) comes from Wikipedia's Tajik SSR page.

era-1920.says: FOTW (tj-ir, Encyclopaedia Iranica text): the Bukharan People's Republic's constitution ratified 23 September 1921 set a flag of green over red with a gold star and crescent and the letters BNSR; in October 1923 the upper stripe became red; the state was abolished in October 1924; the Tajik ASSR constitution of 28 April 1929 set a red flag with arms upper left. Wikipedia (Bukharan People's Soviet Republic): proclaimed 8 October 1920, 1920-24; the flag combined the hammer and sickle with the traditional crescent; its east was given to the Tajik ASSR, which joined the Uzbek SSR as part of it and became a Soviet republic in 1929.
era-1920.open: The two sources describe different flags (FOTW green-over-red then red, with star and crescent; Wikipedia hammer and sickle with crescent) and neither matches the plain hammer-and-sickle red flag on the page. No flag for the Tajik ASSR of 1924-29 is described. The page text was corrected.

era-1500.says: FOTW (uz-bu): the Emirate existed 1785-1920; the national flag 'remains elusive'; the emir's flag (after Trembicki, Flag Bulletin) and a museum flag are green (probably) with a red border and white left hand, crescent and three stars. FOTW (tj-ir, Iranica text): the royal standard, considered the state flag, was light green with gold inscriptions, an open hand, a star and crescent, and an orange border. Wikipedia (Emirate of Bukhara): 1785-1920; flag image captioned as published in 1929 by the deposed emir Sayyid Alim Khan, not described. No Khanate-era flag is described.
era-1500.open: Emirate: both FOTW pages derive from other writers and disagree on the border colour; Wikipedia gives no description, so a second independent description is missing. Khanate (c.1500-1785): no flag found. The page's plain green field with crescent is a simplification.

era-1370.says: Wikipedia (Timurid Empire, 1370-1507): there is 'little certainty about the actual flag'; red banners possibly with a crescent, a black banner with a silver dragon in the Indian campaign and golden dragons before the China campaign are mentioned; the three equal circles in a triangle are the 'sign of Timur' on coins and seals, and a Catalan Atlas flag with three circles may relate to it (Kadoi 2010). A web search found a Wikimedia file page arguing that flag is Yuan rather than Timurid. Neither Tajikistan page covers the Timurids.
era-1370.open: The three-ring device is documented as an emblem on coins and seals, not as a flag; the blue field of the drawing is not supported. No second independent source was fetched. Wikipedia text read to 100,000 of 266,728 characters.

era-1220.says: Wikipedia (Chagatai Khanate): the khanate dates 1227-1347 (west 1347-1403, Moghulistan 1347-1462); a caption on the 1375 Catalan Atlas says 'His cities appear with the Chagatai flag' without describing it. Neither Tajikistan page covers the Mongol conquest (1220) or a banner.
era-1220.open: No source read describes a Chagatai banner; the Mongol conquest date of 1220 is not in the Wikipedia text read (first 100,000 of 199,504 characters). Not a finding that no banner existed.

era-819.says: Wikipedia and FOTW (Tajikistan): the crown on the modern flag is tied to the Samanid dynasty; neither describes a Samanid or suzerain flag. Wikipedia (Black Standard): black was the Abbasid dynastic colour after 750. Wikipedia (Samanid Empire): 819-999; the four sons of Asad ibn Saman were made governors under Abbasid suzerainty in 819 and Ismail Samani made the dynasty effectively independent; no flag or banner colour is described.
era-819.open: No source states a Samanid flag or that they used black; the Abbasid black is documented only as the caliphate's colour. Wikipedia Samanid text read to 100,000 of 199,469 characters.

era-819-1.says: Wikipedia (Black Standard): a quoted historian says Umayyad banners were white and black stayed the Abbasid colour after 750; nothing on Transoxiana specifically.
era-819-1.open: Only Wikipedia's Black Standard article was read; no second source ties white (Umayyad) or black (Abbasid) banners to Transoxiana or to a 'regional flag'; Transoxiana specifically was not searched in a reference work.

era-1964.says: Wikipedia's infobox gives the adoption as 30 June 1964. FOTW: Tanganyika and Zanzibar merged on 26 April 1964 and the union flag recombined the two predecessors, the lower green stripe of Tanganyika's flag taking Zanzibar's blue and the stripes rearranged diagonally; the name Tanzania was adopted 29 October 1964; the 1971 Flag Act gives the flag legal validity from 26 April 1964.
era-1964.open: The sources differ on the day (Wikipedia 30 June 1964, FOTW 26 April 1964 for the union and flag), but agree on 1964; the colour meanings and swatch values were not compared.

era-1700-1.says: This page's own caption calls the image a placeholder: «placeholder maroon field — earliest recorded coastal trade era, no flag survives with confidence».
era-1700-1.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1919.says: Wikipedia: Britain administered Tanganyika Territory from about 1919 under a League of Nations mandate, then as a UN trust territory; its flag in 1923-1961 was a British Red Ensign with the territory emblem; the independence flag of 9 December 1961 was green with a gold-edged black band. FOTW: the mandate was formalised 20 July 1922, trust status from 1946; Red and Blue Ensigns carried a giraffe-head badge (approved 1919) until the end of 1961; the 9 December 1961 flag was green-black-green with thin gold stripes, based on TANU's flag.
era-1919.open: The drawing shows only the 1961 independence flag, the last years of the era; the dates of the Red Ensign differ (Wikipedia 1923, FOTW 1919); the page's colour meanings are covered only for FOTW's 'land, people, minerals' reading.

era-1885.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Tanzania): the German East Africa Company had a flag in 1885-1891 (image only) and the colony's flag in 1891-1918 was a horizontal black-white-red tricolour with the Reichsadler in a white circle. Wikipedia (German East Africa): the colony was established by the DOAG on 27 February 1885, 1885-1918, infobox flag the Colonial Office service flag, a 1914 proposed flag never used. FOTW: DOAG flag from about 1885 (undescribed), governors' flag 1898-1919 black-white-red with the uncrowned imperial eagle in the white stripe; 1914 colonial flags never adopted.
era-1885.open: Both sources describe a tricolour with an eagle (FOTW: the governors' flag), not the black field with a black-white-red canton drawn on this page, so the drawing is not confirmed; whether the tricolour served as the colony's flag generally, and the years (1891 or 1898 start), is unsettled.

era-1700.says: Wikipedia: a plain red flag of Zanzibar under the Omani Empire 1698-1856, then a striped Sultanate flag with eight green crescents 1856-1896. FOTW: Oman flew a plain red flag that continued in use after the Sultan moved his seat to Zanzibar in 1840, and Zanzibar was part of the Sultanate of Oman 'as was much of the East African coast'.
era-1700.open: The two publishers conflict on whether the plain red flag lasted to 1885 (FOTW) or gave way to a striped flag in 1856 (Wikipedia); neither names the Swahili towns or the interior's flags, and FOTW's Zanzibar page does not mention the 1856 flag.

era-1932.says: Wikipedia: 1979 Flag Act proportions 6:9 with blue stripe two parts wide; 30 September 2017 CIELAB standard; blue read as monarchy. FOTW: 1979 Act 6:9 with stripes 1-1-2-1-1; 30 September 2017 colour standard; blue for monarchy, white for Theravada Buddhism, red for land.
era-1932.open: The meanings are unofficial in both sources.

era-6c.says: This page's own caption calls the image a placeholder: «placeholder maroon field — Dvaravati and Khmer-influenced era, no flag survives».
era-6c.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1917.says: Wikipedia: 28 September 1917 middle stripe changed to dark blue; explanations include Allied solidarity and the colour of Vajiravudh's birthday. FOTW: 28 September 1917 stripe changed to blue, reportedly for solidarity with the Allies; Flag Act of 1917 made it the national flag.

era-1782.says: Wikipedia: Rama I decreed a red flag with a white chakra around 1782, Rama II added a white elephant inside it around 1817, Rama IV made the white elephant on red the official flag in 1855, and Vajiravudh changed it in 1916-17. FOTW's historical page reports the same sequence from The History of Thai Flags (Fine Arts Department of Thailand, 1977, quoted by a contributor): chakra 1782, elephant in the chakra 1817, chakra removed and elephant enlarged 1855, caparisoned elephant on 2 November 1916, five red and white stripes in early 1917, blue central stripe on 28 September 1917; Crampton and Poels are cited for the chakra and elephant.
era-1782.open: Dates differ slightly in other FOTW-cited sources (a French tourist site gives 1802 for the elephant and 1851 for removing the chakra); the page's 'plain red field with the white elephant' for the whole period 1782-1917 is a simplification, since the chakra was present until 1855 and the design changed in 1916-1917.

era-1238.says: Wikipedia: Siam used a plain red flag from about 1680 to 1782, probably first under King Narai (1656-88). FOTW's historical page: the first known national flag of Thailand seems to have been a plain red flag, listed for Siam c.1656-1782, and The History of Thai Flags (Fine Arts Department, 1977, quoted by a contributor) says a plain red flag became the national flag on 3 September 1680.
era-1238.open: Neither source covers Sukhothai or the period before about 1656, so the row's 1238 start is unsupported; some flag books cited by FOTW say the first flag was red with a chakra. The 'ship ensign' wording on this page is not in the sources.

era-2002.says: Wikipedia's infobox gives adoption as 1975 (de facto) and 2002 (de jure). Flags of the World (Timor-Leste): the constitutional assembly restored all the symbols of the 1975 independence, the constitution was approved in March 2002 and the flag raised at the 20 May 2002 independence celebrations; (East Timor 1975 flag) the 1975 flag was red with a black triangle, yellow arrowhead and white star, proclaimed by Fretilin on 28 November 1975 (David Rogers), and Zrzavy cites a 1978 source that it is exactly the present flag including the 1:2 ratio.
era-2002.open: The meanings differ: Rogers (1975) gives black for four centuries of colonial oppression, while the 2002 constitution as quoted by FOTW gives yellow as traces of colonialism, black as the obscurantism to be overcome, red as the struggle for national liberation and white as peace; Martins says the 1975 flag was mostly shown at 2:3.

era-14c.says: This page's own caption calls the image a placeholder: «placeholder — pre-colonial Timorese kingdoms, no unifying flag survives».
era-14c.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1999.says: Wikipedia: the UN flag was used during UN administration (1999-2002) and the CNRT flag was chosen at the April 1998 Peniche convention as a provisional national flag, semi-official until 2002; the UN flag was lowered and the national flag raised on 20 May 2002. Flags of the World (UN mandate): contributors found no UNTAET flag, only the UN flag hoisted at the INTERFET handover and at ceremonies in 2000 and 2001, which Kelly says reconfirms its official use; the historical page adds that the CNRT flag was given quasi-official status.
era-1999.open: The card shows a stylised placeholder lettered UN UNTAET rather than the UN flag itself; FOTW does not describe the CNRT flag's design.

era-1975.says: Wikipedia: Indonesian troops replaced the Portuguese flag on Atauro on 30 December 1975; the Indonesian flag was used 1976-1999 and other flags were banned; a provincial flag of Timor Timur (arms on orange) was used only in the governor's office; Fretilin's 28 November 1975 flag was adopted de facto. Flags of the World: integrationists, militias and other pro-Indonesians used exclusively the undefaced Indonesian flag; the Timor Timur provincial flag with the occupation arms on orange was reported by Cahoon but local sources do not confirm it; abroad the territory was symbolised by the Fretilin flag.
era-1975.open: Both sources point to the plain Indonesian red-and-white flag; the red-white-blue flag with a star drawn on the card is not described by either, and the provincial flag is attested only as reported.

era-1702.says: Wikipedia: Portuguese Timor used only the flag of Portugal and had no separate colonial flag, with Portuguese designs dated 1702-07, 1830-1910 and 1910-75; proposals for a Timor flag in 1932 and 1965 were never adopted. Flags of the World (historical flags): Portuguese flags were used in forts and factories, military or Dominican flags may have been used, and Martins knows of no local tribal flags.
era-1702.open: The Portuguese flag changed over the span (WP's dated designs); the card shows only the 1910 Portuguese design, and the page's earlier wording of a territory banner is not supported.

era-1960.says: Both sources give 1960, the year this page starts the current flag. Wikipedia's infobox gives the adoption as 27 April 1960; Flags of the World dates it 27 April 1960.
era-1960.open: Only the year the current flag was adopted was compared; the design and the swatch colours were not checked against a specification.

era-1884.says: Wikipedia says Germany's flag was used in German Togoland from 1884 to 1914, without distinguishing imperial and colonial flags. Flags of the World says Togo was a German colony until the German administration surrendered on 26 August 1914; its page on German colonies (summarising Schurdel and others) says civil ships and often official buildings flew the black-white-red national flag, the naval ensign was used at hoistings and by troops, and a service flag is visible in a Lome photograph; its page on the 1914 colonial flags says the colonial arms-bearing flags (Togo's shield showed two snakes and a palm tree) were designed in 1914 but never introduced because of the war.
era-1884.open: The national flag was not the only flag: the naval ensign and the Reich service flag were also used, and the page's 'colonial ensign with a territorial badge' was a 1914 design never introduced (so it did not fly). FOTW's list gives Togo as 1884 to August 1914.

era-1970.says: Both sources date the current flag to 1875, before this era begins in 1970, so the flag was already in use at the start. Wikipedia's infobox gives the adoption as 4 November 1875; Flags of the World dates it November 1875.
era-1970.open: Only the year the current flag was adopted was compared; the design and the swatch colours were not checked against a specification.

era-1900.says: FOTW (to.html): Tonga was a British Protected State from 18 May 1900 to 4 June 1970; the flag, enshrined in the constitution of 4 November 1875, remained in use during that period (Southworth); David Prothero is quoted that Protected States did not have Blue Ensigns or defaced Union Jacks; older sources show the flag at 2:3 and the current image is 1:2. Wikipedia (Kingdom of Tonga 1900-1970): a protected state under the Treaty of Friendship of 18 May 1900 until independence on 4 June 1970, its infobox showing the Flag of Tonga. Wikipedia (Flag of Tonga): the constitution says the flag can never be altered.
era-1900.open: Wikipedia's evidence is the infobox image only; the statement that protected states had no Blue Ensign is Prothero via FOTW alone. The proportion change (2:3 to 1:2) has no date.

era-1845.says: Wikipedia: a 4 November 1875 constitution codified the flag (red field, white canton with a red Greek cross); the early white flag with a red cross resembled the Red Cross emblem (adopted 1863) and was changed to a canton on red. FOTW: 1862 first design a white flag with a red cross, changed to a canton on red after the 1863 Red Cross; the constitution of 4 November 1875 (section 47) says it shall never be altered; one contributor says the present flag was decreed in 1866.
era-1845.open: The two sources read give 1862 and 1866 as earlier dates for the design; the 'contemporary international convention' wording and 'unaltered ever since' (FOTW notes proportions varied) are not in either.

era-1962.says: Both sources give 1962, the year this page starts the current flag. Wikipedia's infobox gives the adoption as 31 August 1962; Flags of the World dates it 1962.
era-1962.open: Only the year the current flag was adopted was compared; the design and the swatch colours were not checked against a specification.

era-5000bce.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1889.says: Wikipedia: before independence in 1962 the colony used a British blue ensign defaced with a badge of a ship arriving in front of a mountain (its captions list a colonial flag and a red ensign for 1889-1958 and 1958-1962), and its history article says the two islands were incorporated into one entity in 1889. FOTW's colonial flags page (David Prothero): the Blue Ensign badge was introduced for Trinidad in 1875, in 1889 Tobago was annexed to Trinidad and the Trinidad badge became the badge of Trinidad and Tobago, used on the Blue Ensign until 1958 and then replaced by the same scene in a shield with a motto scroll.
era-1889.open: FOTW says there was no official Red Ensign with this badge (only an unofficial one reported), whereas Wikipedia's captions list a red ensign; the 1958 shield badge and the 1959 flag are not on this page. Tobago's separate badge (1876-1889) is in FOTW's Tobago page.

era-1797.says: Wikipedia's history: Trinidad was surrendered to the British in 1797; Tobago was confirmed British by the 1814 Treaty of Paris; the islands were incorporated in 1889. FOTW's Tobago page: Tobago was occupied by Britain in 1797, a colony from 1814 and separate until 1888/89, and 'used British ensigns with a badge' (a blue ensign with badge from 1877, a badge from 1876 per Prothero); FOTW's colonial page dates the Trinidad Blue Ensign badge to 1875.
era-1797.open: The two publishers support the dates but badge-defaced ensigns are dated only from 1870-1877 in FOTW; no source read gives the flag over Trinidad or Tobago in 1797-1870, so the single British colonial ensign drawn for the whole span is not established.

era-1498.says: Wikipedia's history article: Columbus sighted Trinidad in 1498 and claimed it for Spain, and it was administered by Spain until 1797. FOTW's Spanish pages date the Burgundy cross as a Spanish ensign from 1506 to the 1670s and a jack until 1785, call it a military banner rather than the official flag of the Spanish Empire, and make royal arms on white the ensign from about 1701.
era-1498.open: No source read ties the Cross of Burgundy to Trinidad; FOTW's dates for the cross start in 1506 and end as an ensign in the 1670s, so 'Spain's standard colonial and maritime banner throughout Spanish rule' is not established. Tobago's contested ownership before 1763 is not covered by this row.

era-1956.says: Wikipedia: the flag was proclaimed the state flag of the Republic of Tunisia on 1 June 1959 under Article 4 of the constitution, and the Organic Law of 30 June 1999 (adopted 3 July) formalised it for the first time in law. Flags of the World: the national flag was legislated in the Constitution on 1 June 1959, and the current version, with a slightly adapted crescent, was set by the flag law of 30 June 1999 (published 6 July 1999).
era-1956.open: The two sources differ on when the design began (Wikipedia 1827 or 1831, FOTW 1835). The 'unchanged since 1831' and the 2014 constitution wording are not covered; both sources say the 1999 law clarified the design, and Wikipedia says the crescent was slightly thinner from 1959 to 1999.

era-800.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.
