era-1206.says: Wikipedia (Tug): a tug or sulde is a pole topped with horsetail hair of varying colours; the white banner was a peacetime symbol and the black one a wartime symbol, the original white banner disappeared early and the black survived as the repository of Genghis Khan's soul; a 15th-century Rashid al-Din manuscript shows white banners at his proclamation as Khagan. FOTW: chronicles describe white and black banners with nine tails, white sacred; it calls modern reconstructions of Genghis Khan's banners very doubtful.
era-1206.open: Neither source gives a fixed design or a date for the banner's adoption; the 1206 date comes only from an image file name, not the article text.

era-1240.says: FOTW (mn-early): the 1375 Catalan Atlas shows a silver flag with an engrailed fly and two red charges, a crescent and a simplified tamga, over Sarai, Tana and Urgench, a variant of the 'Emperor of Sarai' flag in the Libro del conoscimiento; FOTW warns it is unclear whether the flags were used. Wikipedia (Catalan Atlas): the Golden Horde symbol is similar to a tamgha, a sign found on Golden Horde coinage until about Jani Beg, with no colours given. Wikipedia (Golden Horde): c.1225/1242-1502; the name is first known from the 1565 History of Kazan ('golden' perhaps for golden tents, wealth or imperial status); the infobox banner is dated 1339 and a caption notes a banner adopted 1267-1280 under Mongke Temur; the Great Horde by 1466 gave rise to the Kazan, Astrakhan and Crimean khanates.
era-1240.open: The Atlas flag is documented by two publishers, but as a map depiction of uncertain use, and the page's white-and-black reconstruction matches neither description. Wikipedia Golden Horde text read to 100,000 of 294,940 characters.

era-1225.says: FOTW (mn-early): the 1375 Catalan Atlas shows a white flag with a gold square in the centre (engrailed fly) over Chagatai cities, with a caveat that the flags may not reflect real use. Wikipedia (Catalan Atlas): cities in the Chagatai realm are shown with the Chagatai flag, no colours or symbols described. Wikipedia (Chagatai Khanate): 1227-1347 as a whole, the west to 1403 and Moghulistan to 1462.
era-1225.open: The atlas depiction is documented by two publishers, but only FOTW describes it and neither shows it was used; the page's blue-and-gold drawing is not described by any source. Wikipedia Chagatai text read to 100,000 of 199,504 characters.

era-1256.says: FOTW (mn-early): the 1375 Catalan Atlas shows a golden flag with a red square in the centre over Ilkhanate cities (Kerman, Qeshm, Bukhara, Samarkand), the page remarking it is in fact the flag of Persia from the Libro del conoscimiento, with a caveat on real use. Wikipedia (Catalan Atlas): Ilkhanate flags appear on the ruler's realm and on ships in the Indian Ocean, undescribed; Wikipedia (Ilkhanate): 1256-1335, with a remnant ended by Jani Beg's conquest of Tabriz in 1357, and a Catalan Atlas caption noting a possible depiction of the Ilkhan.
era-1256.open: Only FOTW describes the colours; Wikipedia gives no design. Neither shows the atlas flags were used, and the page's green-and-gold drawing matches no source. Wikipedia Ilkhanate text read to 100,000 of 251,556 characters.

era-1271.says: Wikipedia (Tug): a Japanese scroll reportedly shows a black banner on the Yuan fleet in the 1274/1281 invasions of Japan. Wikipedia (Catalan Atlas) and Wikipedia (Yuan dynasty): the Catalan Atlas shows a flag with three red crescent moons across the Great Khan's territory; the Yuan article dates the dynasty 1271-1368 (name proclaimed 5 November 1271, Dadu fell 14 September 1368) and describes no Yuan flag. FOTW (mn-early) has no Yuan section; its circa 1310 Mongol flag (from Znamierowski) is not identified as Yuan.
era-1271.open: No source describes a red-and-gold court banner. The three-crescent flag is a map depiction, and the black fleet banner is reportedly from one scroll; all Wikipedia, so neither is independently confirmed. Wikipedia Yuan text read to 100,000 of 272,711 characters.

era-14.says: Wikipedia gives separate end dates: Ilkhanate 1256-1335 (remnant ended 1357); Yuan 1271-1368 (Dadu fell 14 September 1368, Northern Yuan to 1635); Chagatai Khanate whole 1227-1347 with a western part to 1403 and Moghulistan to 1462; Golden Horde ended 1502 (called the Great Horde by 1466, with the Kazan, Astrakhan and Crimean khanates as successors). Wikipedia (Tug) says tugs were later used in derived Turco-Mongol khanates.
era-14.open: All dates are from Wikipedia (one publisher) and no source links the period to a gold field as the colour of imperial authority; the plain gold field remains a placeholder. Wikipedia pages were read only to the first 100,000 characters.

era-1370.says: This page's own caption calls the image a placeholder: «placeholder — no surviving Timurid national flag; Timur's own tamga (a trefoil of three rings) is attested on his tomb and coinage, not as a».
era-1370.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1803.says: Wikipedia's Flags of the Mughal Empire does not discuss 1803-1857. Wikipedia's Bahadur Shah II article says the emperor was pensioned by the Company, allowed to collect taxes in Delhi and keep a force there, and the empire had shrunk to Delhi; it describes no personal flag (a gallery caption shows a generic alam). FOTW does not cover the period.
era-1803.open: No source read describes a Mughal flag or Company colours for the rump period; the 1803 date itself is not given in the Bahadur Shah II article.

era-1707.says: Wikipedia: alam primarily moss green with a lion and sun; at Asaf-ud-Daulah's funeral in 1797 a green Mughal flag was raised higher than the Awadh flag; a needs-citations banner is on the article. Down To Earth says flags of the late 17th century matched earlier descriptions. FOTW shows a lion with the sun on the imperial standard, undated and uncoloured.
era-1707.open: Neither publisher says whether any flag changed after Aurangzeb's death in 1707; the 1797 episode is Wikipedia alone, and the gold sun/star device in the drawing is not what Wikipedia describes.

era-1658.says: Wikipedia: the alam was primarily moss green with a lion and sun; a painting of Aurangzeb's 1705 expedition shows flags and another image triangular green flags; a seal on a 1689 firman. FOTW shows a lion with sun on the imperial standard. Down To Earth does not mention Aurangzeb, but says late 17th-century flags matched earlier descriptions.
era-1658.open: No second publisher describes a flag specific to Aurangzeb's reign or its colour; FOTW gives no dates or colours.

era-1628.says: Wikipedia: Padshahnama paintings of Shah Jahan's reign show scarlet pennons with green borders bearing a lion with a rising sun, and a green field with a couchant lion and rising sun; red and green standards at the 1631 Kandahar siege. Down To Earth (citing Padshahnama paintings of 1631 and 1655) describes scarlet pennants with green borders at the 1631 siege of Qandahar and standards with a green field in a 1655 painting, and says the lion-and-sun appears prominently on the imperial flag from Jahangir's time on. FOTW shows a lion with the sun on the imperial standard, without colours or dates.
era-1628.open: The sources describe more than one design (scarlet-with-green-border pennants and green-field standards), so no single fixed flag for the reign is established; the page's plain green alam is one of them.

era-1556.says: Wikipedia: the Ain-i-Akbari records at least five alams carried with Akbar; Edward Terry (1655) describes a Jahangir silk standard with a crouching lion partly covering the sun. Down To Earth also relies on Terry (who was at Jahangir's court 1615-1619) for the lion-and-sun standard, and says Akbar-era flags showed only a radiant sun on a triangular flag. FOTW shows a lion with the sun on the imperial standard, undated and uncoloured.
era-1556.open: For Akbar the sources disagree on the device (Wikipedia: lion and sun traced back to Timur; Down To Earth: only a radiant sun); the colour (green) is not stated for either reign by a second publisher. The drawing is a reconstruction.

era-1526.says: WP: alam primarily moss green with a lion and sun, use traced back to Timur; seals for Babur (1527) and Humayun. FOTW names Babur as founder with no date or flag detail.
era-1526.open: Reign-specific flags for Babur and Humayun are not described.

era-1000.says: This page's own caption calls the image a placeholder: «placeholder — no attested Norse or indigenous national banner».
era-1000.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1949.says: Wikipedia: the Union Flag was readopted as the provincial flag in 1949 and stayed official until 1980, when the House of Assembly approved Christopher Pratt's design. FOTW's history page (citing Public Record Office papers): union with Canada took effect 31 March 1949 with no immediate effect on flags, the Revised Statutes of 1952 (chapter 272) retained the Red and Blue Ensigns and reaffirmed the Union Jack as the 'national flag', the ensigns were discontinued in 1965, and the Union Jack remained the provincial flag until the present flag was chosen by the House of Assembly on 28 May 1980, given royal assent on 6 June and first raised 24 June.
era-1949.open: The sources give slightly different 1980 dates (Wikipedia: approved 28 May, first flown 24 June; FOTW's main page: adoption 6 June, first raising 23 or 24 June) and the Canadian Red Ensign is not shown by either as the provincial flag; the end of the 1949 era at 1980 on this page is a design choice of the page.

era-1934.says: Wikipedia: the National Flag Act of 1931 made the Union Flag the national flag until 1949, with the Red Ensign for merchant ships and the Blue Ensign for government ships. FOTW's history page: the National Flag Act took effect 15 May 1931 and reduced the planned three national flags to one, the Union Jack; the legislature asked in 1933 for the constitution to be suspended and Commissioners took office in 1934, ending Dominion status; the Union Jack stayed the 'national flag' through the 1949 union and the 1952 statutes.
era-1934.open: Both sources date the Union Jack as national flag from 1931, not 1934; the 1934 start of this row is the start of the Commission of Government only, and the sources contradict the page's earlier statement that the Union Jack replaced the Red Ensign in 1934.

era-1907.says: Wikipedia: Newfoundland became a Dominion in 1907 without formally adopting an ensign; the Red and Blue Ensigns bearing the Great Seal were official from 1904 to 1931 and the Red Ensign was widely treated as the national flag. FOTW's history page: the 1904 badge (the allegorical scene from the colony's seal, approved 18 May 1904) appeared on the Governor's Union Jack and the government Blue Ensign, and was approved for the Red Ensign on 25 October 1918; from 1918 to 1965 Newfoundland flew the British Red Ensign with the badge on the fly as a merchant ensign.
era-1907.open: The sources differ on dates: Wikipedia has the Dominion from 1907, FOTW says Dominion status was granted in 1917; Wikipedia says the ensigns were official to 1931 while FOTW has the Red Ensign as a merchant ensign to 1965. Both place the national flag as the Union Jack from 1931, so this row's end at 1934 is not supported.

era-1610.says: Wikipedia: the Red Ensign with a colonial badge became the colony's civil ensign in the Victorian era (no exact date) and Parliament designated a Newfoundland ensign in 1904. FOTW's history page documents instead: an 1862 watercolour of a flag at Government House, St John's (a St George's cross with a crown on white), a Governor's Union Jack and government Blue Ensign with a crown and 'Terra Nova' badge on a white disc from 1870 (approved 28 September 1870), the 1904 badge, and arms granted in 1638 and forgotten until 1924.
era-1610.open: FOTW dates the Red Ensign with the Newfoundland badge only from 1918 and the pre-1904 badge appears on the Blue Ensign and Governor's flag, so the page's Red Ensign with a badge for the colony is not established by two publishers; nothing read covers 1610-1862.

era-1299.says: This page's own caption calls the image a placeholder: «placeholder — Osman I's small frontier beylik, no fixed banner survives».
era-1299.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1922.says: Flags of the World (Turkey): apart from design specifications, nothing changed when the Ottoman Empire became the Republic of Turkey and the caliphate ended, and the 1936 law adopted the 1844 Ottoman design without alteration. Flags of the World (Ottoman Empire): empire ended 1 November 1922 when the sultanate was eliminated; republic proclaimed 29 October 1923. Wikipedia: empire abolished 1922; caliphate standard of Abdulmejid II 19 November 1922 - 3 March 1924; Turkish Flag Law 29 May 1936.
era-1922.open: Pointer era: the 1922-1923 flag is not separately described; Wikipedia does not date the republic; the drawing links to the Turkey page for the republic's flag.

era-1844.says: Wikipedia: 1844 official adoption of the red flag with white crescent and five-pointed star (Tanzimat), after an eight-pointed-star flag 1793-1844; a footnote gives a rival claim of 1826 under Mahmud II. Flags of the World (Turkey): the basic form was established in 1793 under Selim III (green navy flags changed to red, white crescent and star added) and 'the five-pointed star dates from approximately 1844'; the 1936 Turkish law adopted the 1844 Ottoman design unaltered. Flags of the World (Ottoman Empire) flags its own 1793/1844 dates from Znamierowski as unevidenced and notes 1857 and 1905 charts show a five-pointed star. Flags of the World's 19th-century chart page gives no 1844 date and shows charts with six-pointed (Steenbergen 1862) and eight-pointed (Webster 1884) stars.
era-1844.open: Both sources date the five-pointed star to about 1844, but FOTW treats it as 'approximately' and unevidenced, Wikipedia has a rival 1826 claim, and a contributor recorded a seven-pointed star on one chart; the two sources may share one origin (Znamierowski). The 1922 end date and the claim that the flag is still Turkey's are covered under the 1922 row.

era-1517.says: Wikipedia: Zulfiqar war flags common in the 16th-17th centuries, star-and-crescent reported at Mohacs 1526 and Vienna 1683, a 1613 naval flag green with white crescent, an 1793 decree for a red star-and-crescent navy flag. Flags of the World agrees on the red Zulfikar flags (Selim I's red sandjak in Topkapi; red Zulfikar flags widespread in the 16th-17th centuries, citing the Encyclopaedia of Islam and Kilicbay 1999) and shows the two 1613 naval flags from Madrid (green with white crescent; white with red stripes and red crescent); its Turkey page says the red flag with white crescent and star was established apparently in 1793 when green navy flags were changed to red.
era-1517.open: Two publishers agree on red Zulfikar war flags and green and white crescent naval flags before 1793, but neither supports a plain red crescent banner as the empire's flag across 1517-1844, so the page's caption and drawing are not confirmed; no source describes a land state flag of the period.

era-1453.says: Wikipedia: a simple crescent flag 'from its foundation in 1453', Babinger on a possible Byzantine origin of the star and crescent, and Selim I's Zulfiqar flag in the 1510s. Flags of the World (Zulfikar flags) shows Selim I's red sandjak (he reigned 1512-1520) and says it is in the Topkapi Museum, and its Turkey page links the crescent and star to Byzantium; nothing is dated 1453-1512.
era-1453.open: No source states a plain red imperial banner for 1453-1517; only the 1510s red Zulfikar standard is documented for the end of the span, and the Byzantine origin of the crescent is reported as a possibility.

era-1362.says: Wikipedia: the horse-tail tugh was the early Ottoman military symbol and a 1721 source puts a crescent on infantry standards under Orhan (1324-1360). Flags of the World (18th-century page) shows the horse-tail standard (Thou or Thouy) from Tournefort (1718) and Picart (1737) and its Zulfikar page describes a light green Barbarossa standard from Suleiman's reign (16th century).
era-1362.open: The tugh is attested by two publishers, but as a later (18th-century) record; no source dates a green battle standard to 1362-1453, and the Barbarossa standard is 16th-century.

era-2700bce.says: This page's own caption calls the image a placeholder: «placeholder — no attested banner; pre-vexillological ancient kingdom».
era-2700bce.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-633.says: Wikipedia: Arab-Muslim forces captured the derafsh after the Battle of al-Qadisiyyah (no year given). FOTW (pre-Islamic flags): the banner was lost to the Arabs at Qadisiyya, dated A.D. 637 in one footnote and about 636 from Preble's chronology; size about 22 by 15 feet; Preble says the captor received thirty thousand pieces of gold.
era-633.open: The era's flag content is the loss of the derafsh at Qadisiyya, which the two sources date to c. 636-637, outside the 633-651 span's endpoints; neither states the Sasanian fall in 651 as a flag event. Encyclopaedia Iranica was blocked (403) and not worked around.

era-224.says: Wikipedia: the derafsh was the official standard of the Sasanian Empire (224-651), bejewelled, with a star emblem; the lead image is an artist's rendition. FOTW: Sasanian use is 'purported', later Sasanian coins do not show it, and no image survives so all depictions are reconstructions; Qadisiyyah dated 636 or 637.
era-224.open: The page's 636 date is one of two dates given by FOTW; the apron legend is from the Shahnameh (10th century) and its antiquity is not established.

era-247bce.says: Wikipedia: a scholar suggests the Parthian imperial standard 'seems to have been' the derafsh. FOTW: the flag-like device appears on coins of the Persis fratarakas (3rd-2nd centuries BCE) under Seleucid and Arsacid rule, vanishing by the end of the 2nd century BCE. Neither describes a horse-and-bow standard.
era-247bce.open: The Parthian bow-and-horse cavalry standard drawn here is not covered by any source read.

era-312bce.says: Wikipedia: Iranian coins of the 3rd and 2nd centuries BCE show the derafsh, including one of Baydad, a Persis governor under the Seleucids. FOTW: fratarakas' flag-like standard on coins under Seleucid and Parthian rule, possibly 'vexilloids'.
era-312bce.open: The Seleucid anchor device as a standard, and the 312 BCE start, are not covered by the sources read.

era-334bce.says: Neither source covers Alexander's conquest. Wikipedia (Faravahar): the symbol was not present in much Persian art after the Achaemenids. FOTW lists no Alexander-era flag.
era-334bce.open: The 330 BCE date and the claim of symbolic absorption are not covered.

era-550bce.says: Wikipedia (Faravahar): the winged-disc figure is on Persepolis reliefs and the tombs of Darius (r. 522-486 BC) and Artaxerxes III, derived from Assyrian winged-disc iconography, meaning debated, not said to be a flag. Wikipedia (Derafsh Kaviani): Xenophon says a golden eagle was the Achaemenid standard. FOTW (pre-Islamic flags) quotes G.H. Preble that Cyrus adopted, according to Herodotus and Xenophon, a golden eagle with outstretched wings on a white flag; FOTW gives no date and does not mention the faravahar.
era-550bce.open: The golden-eagle standard is secondhand on both pages (Xenophon via Wikipedia, Preble via FOTW) and no reference source was reached (Encyclopaedia Iranica's derafsh entry returned 403 and was not worked around); whether the faravahar was ever a flag is not established, and the drawing is a reconstruction.

era-753bce.says: This page's own caption calls the image a placeholder: «placeholder — the legendary Kingdom of Rome, no banner survives».
era-753bce.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1000bce.says: This page's own caption calls the image a placeholder: «placeholder — scattered Iron Age hut villages, no polity or banner yet».
era-1000bce.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1453.says: Wikipedia: Constantinople was captured by the Ottoman Empire on 29 May 1453 after a 53-day siege under Sultan Mehmed II, ending the Byzantine Empire. Flags of the World's Byzantine page: Michael VIII Palaiologos retook Constantinople in 1261 and his descendants held the throne until the city and the Empire fell to the Ottomans in 1453.
era-1453.open: This is a pointer card: the two sources date the event and the succession but describe no flag raised or lowered at the fall.

era-330.says: Flags of the World: 'The Byzantine Imperial flag is yellow with a black crowned double-headed eagle', 'the symbol of the Palaiologos' (1258-1453), first made by an emperor Komnenos, crowns added by the Palaiologoi (one for Nikaia, one for Constantinople after 1261), with the yellow-black the peacetime flag; the 14th-century Book of All Kingdoms shows Byzantine flags. Wikipedia: the double-headed eagle is not securely attested with the emperor before the 1301 chrysobull of Andronikos II (Soloviev c. 1288) and was used by the Palaiologan emperors for senior imperial family members; Pseudo-Kodinos (mid-14th c.) calls the tetragrammatic cross the customary imperial banner.
era-330.open: The two publishers agree on a Palaiologan double-headed eagle but differ on whether it was the flag (FOTW) or an emblem beside the cross banner (Wikipedia), and on its origin (Komnenos vs not before 1301). Neither covers 330-1261 or says the eagle descends from the aquila; the card is a later-form reconstruction.

era-395.says: Wikipedia (Western Roman Empire): after Theodosius I died on 17 January 395 the empire was divided between his sons Honorius (West) and Arcadius (East), and Romulus Augustulus was deposed by Odoacer on 4 September 476. Wikipedia's Byzantine flags page says the vexillum and draco are still occasionally attested in the 5th century and beyond. The World History Encyclopedia page on the Western empire was read but does not mention a 395 partition or any flags.
era-395.open: The 395 and 476 dates rest on Wikipedia alone (World History Encyclopedia dates the end to 476 but not the 395 split); no source describes the standards of either half, so the claim that both continued Roman legionary symbolism is only the general Wikipedia statement.

era-284.says: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Antiquities (J. Yates, 1875): after Constantine embraced Christianity 'a figure or emblem of Christ, woven in gold upon purple cloth' was substituted for the emperor's head on the standard, which 'was called labarum' (Prudentius, Nicephorus). Flags of the World: the emblem Constantine bore was the only recognised Christian emblem of his time, the Greek X and P, and the labarum was made of silk. Wikipedia (Labarum): Constantine's vision before the Milvian Bridge is dated 27 October 312 with differing accounts; little evidence for the labarum before c. 317; Wikipedia (Vexillum): Constantine replaced the spear point with the Chi-Rho.
era-284.open: Smith does not name the Chi-Rho; no source says the labarum replaced the older pagan legionary standards; the Tetrarchy (284-312) is not covered; the 312 vision is told differently by Lactantius and Eusebius. The card is a reconstruction.

era-27bce.says: Smith's Dictionary (J. Yates, 1875): 'In the second consulship of Marius, B.C. 104, the four quadrupeds were entirely laid aside as standards, the eagle being alone retained'; the eagle was of silver or bronze with expanded wings, and under later emperors it was carried with the legion. Wikipedia (Aquila): each legion carried one aquila; the Marius origin after 104 BC is Pliny's claim and disputed; bulls and wolves were also used by late Republican and early Imperial legions. Flags of the World mentions an aquila only as a modern re-enactment piece.
era-27bce.open: SPQR on the aquila is stated by none of the sources (Smith does not mention SPQR; Wikipedia's Vexillum doubts SPQR on army standards), so the card's caption detail is unsupported; no Imperial-era aquila survives.

era-509bce.says: Smith's Dictionary (Yates, 1875): the standards of the manipuli or smaller divisions of the cohort were called vexilla, borne by vexillarii; it describes a scarlet flag only in a Greek battle-signal context and does not tie the vexillum to the Republic or mention SPQR. Wikipedia (Vexillum): a red vexillum with yellow SPQR is 'sometimes reported' but unsourced and no evidence of SPQR on army flags is found; the only surviving vexillum is of the 3rd century AD. Flags of the World: the vexillum was a cloth on a crossbar, SPQR was never used on flags in antiquity, and Suetonius records a blue vexillum awarded to Marcus Agrippa after a naval victory.
era-509bce.open: The vexillum as a Roman cloth standard is supported by all three, but nothing read dates a particular design (red, SPQR) to 509-27 BC; the Agrippa blue vexillum (a decoration, undated in the text read) is the only late-Republic vexillum named.

era-1187.says: This page's own caption calls the image a placeholder: «placeholder — rival gusuku lords and, later, three separate kingdoms, no shared banner».
era-1187.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1879.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Okinawa Prefecture): the prefectural emblem became official on 15 May 1972 and the flag on 13 October 1972, and under US rule only the US flag was permitted; Wikipedia (Ryukyu Kingdom): Okinawa Prefecture was established in 1879. Wikipedia (Flag of Japan) and Flags of the World (Japan): the sun disc flag was proclaimed for merchant ships and the navy in 1870 and served as Japan's national flag, legally to 1885 and by custom until the 1999 law.
era-1879.open: No source says when the Japanese flag began to fly in Okinawa, and 1945-1972 under US rule is excluded by Wikipedia, so a continuous 1879-present display of Japan's flag is not established.

era-1872.says: Wikipedia (Ryukyu Domain): the domain lasted 1872-1879 with Sho Tai as Domain King, and its infobox captions an image 'Flag of Ryukyu Domain' with the Second Sho family emblem; the text mentions no Japanese flag. Flags of the World (Ryukyu flags, Kariyasu, 2025): no document or drawing of a Ryukyu national flag was found; Ryukyu used ship flags with the Sho three-comma emblem; a white flag with a three-colour comma design is likely post-1945.
era-1872.open: No source says Japan's flag flew over the domain or calls it a legal fiction; the sources instead point to a Sho emblem flag.

era-1609.says: Wikipedia: the hidari mitsudomoe crest is called the first historical national symbol; Daisaku Kina (2012) found no contemporary source showing it used as a national flag, and ships bound for Satsuma after 1609 flew a banner with the Sho crest; a flag labelled 'flag of Ryukyu' from a ship drifting to Choshi in 1798 had a white field and black mitsudomoe. FOTW: no document or drawing of a national flag was found; a white flag with red, blue and yellow commas was probably invented after WWII; ship flags show the Sho three-comma emblem in both orientations.
era-1609.open: The sources do not say a flag was absent; they report none found. The red field shown here is not supported (sources describe white fields), so the drawing is a symbolic stand-in.

era-1429.says: Wikipedia: King Sho Toku adopted the hidari mitsudomoe in 1467 (a coffin inscribed with it and the year 1500 corroborates use); it does not describe any 1429 flag. Wikipedia and FOTW both report no document showing a national flag.
era-1429.open: The crest is dated after 1429 by the source, so it is not shown to be in use from the start of this era; the sources report no flag found rather than proving none existed.

era-1921-1.says: This page's own caption calls the image a placeholder: «placeholder maroon field — pre-republic era, no distinct territorial banner survives».
era-1921-1.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-200bce.says: This page's own caption calls the image a placeholder: «placeholder — no unified banner from any of the successive steppe polities».
era-200bce.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1944.says: Wikipedia and FOTW agree: Tuva was absorbed on 11 October 1944 and local flags and arms were abolished; Wikipedia says the Tuvan Autonomous Oblast had no flag of its own (the RSFSR flag is shown for 1944-1954) and the Republic of Tuva has had its own flag since 17 September 1992. FOTW's Soviet-era page says the Tuvan ASSR (10 October 1961) flag was the RSFSR flag with a gold Russian inscription (law of 10 January 1962), with a Tuvan inscription from 1978.
era-1944.open: The drawing shows a white-blue-red tricolour; neither source says it flew in Tuva, and for 1944-92 both point to the RSFSR (Soviet red) flag with inscriptions, so the drawing needs redrawing. The post-1992 flag is not drawn.

era-1943.says: Wikipedia: the last Tuvan People's Republic flag ran 8 September 1943 - 11 October 1944, with the initials in Cyrillic, and a possible hammer-and-sickle variant. FOTW (after Sokolov in the Flag Bulletin): the constitution of 25 June 1941 set a red flag, 1:2, with the state initials 'TAR' in gold in the canton; Cyrillic letters came on 8 September 1943 and the initials became 'TAP' by custom, not by law.
era-1943.open: A red flag with gold initials in the canton is established by both sources; the blue canton and cross-and-sun device drawn here are not described by either (FOTW's Sokolov-based account contradicts a blue canton). The drawing needs redrawing.

era-1921.says: Wikipedia: independence proclaimed 14 August 1921; an unofficial flag for 1921-1926 known only from reconstructions; first official flag 24 November 1926 - 18 October 1930 with the name in Mongol script. FOTW (after Sokolov): plain red party flags in 1921, the 1926 constitution set a red flag with the state arms in the centre, with revised arms in 1930, 1933 and 1941; a blue flag with a gold emblem for 1918-21 is reported by Crampton and doubted by FOTW contributors.
era-1921.open: Both sources give red flags with arms from 1926 and plain red in 1921; the drawn blue field with a gold monogram canton matches only the doubted 1918-21 report and is not supported for 1921-43.

era-1958.says: Wikipedia says the constitutions of 1946 and 1958 named the blue, white and red flag as the national emblem, quoting Article 2 of 1958: «the national emblem is the tricolour flag, blue, white, red»; that President Giscard d'Estaing introduced a lighter blue in 1974; and that on 13 July 2020 President Macron reverted the Élysée Palace to the darker hue without a statement. FOTW, citing the Société française de vexillologie, gives the same Article 2 wording for 1958, 1974 and 1976 for the lightening (Sache gives 1976), and 13 July 2020 for the darker blue, which it says was not officially announced and was mainly seen on state buildings.
era-1958.open: The sources date the lightening to 1974 or 1976. Neither names a shade, so the swatch colours are approximations. This is a start-year check only for the constitutional text; the flag itself dates from 1794.

era-1944.says: Wikipedia: the constitutions of 1946 and 1958 instituted the blue, white and red flag as the national emblem of the Republic (1958 art. 2: 'the national emblem is the tricolour flag, blue, white, red'). Flags of the World (Third Republic page): a tricolour that had been the last flown in Paris in 1940 was raised again on 19 August 1944; its Fourth Republic page shows the tricolour and gives no dated change in these years.
era-1944.open: No source read describes a Provisional Government flag distinct from the tricolour, and the Fourth Republic is covered only by the 1946 constitution reference; the abbreviation 'PFG' in FOTW's account is unexpanded.

era-1940.says: FOTW says the French State kept the tricolour (Stilling and Müller), that its only new flag was the head of state's standard, prescribed by a decree of 19 March 1942 as a tricolour with seven gold stars on the white stripe below a francisque (du Payrat and Blanc), and that Free France had to add a charge to the tricolour because Vichy kept it, the cross of Lorraine being prescribed as its emblem by a regulation of 5 June 1941 (Sache). Wikipedia's captions say Pétain used a standard with a francisque in the white stripe and the Free French a cross of Lorraine in the white stripe, and its Free France article says Vice-Admiral Muselier created the naval jack with a red cross of Lorraine by general order no. 2 of 3 July 1940 and that d'Argenlieu suggested the cross.
era-1940.open: The sources differ on when the cross of Lorraine was adopted (June 1940 or July 1940 for the jack, 5 June 1941 for the regulation) and on who proposed it (Muselier, d'Argenlieu). Neither describes the cross-of-Lorraine flags in enough detail to draw, and the image shows the plain tricolour. The star colour on Pétain's standard is gold in the decree and blue in a 1941 scout book.

era-1870.says: Wikipedia says the Comte de Chambord demanded a white flag as a condition of accepting the throne, rejected it when offered the throne in 1870, and that the tricolour was kept. FOTW says Chambord insisted on the white flag with fleurs-de-lis in the dispute of 1873, that compromise ideas were a tricolour with fleurs-de-lis or a white flag with a tricolour cravat, and that he held out.
era-1870.open: The sources differ on the year of the dispute (1870 or 1873). Neither gives a law fixing the flag under the Third Republic.

era-1852.says: Flags of the World: Louis-Napoleon was proclaimed Emperor as Napoleon III on 2 December 1852 and the national flag was the blue-white-red tricolour; its main France page says a regulation of 17 May 1853 officialised the 30:33:37 optical proportions for the ensign and that the dark navy blue was established at least from the Second Empire. Wikipedia: the navy flag regulation of 17 May 1853 returned the stripes to 30:33:37, and the Third Republic followed the overthrow of Napoleon III.
era-1852.open: Wikipedia does not tie the 1853 regulation to the Second Empire in words, only by date; the imperial bee as an emblem is FOTW's alone.

era-1848.says: Wikipedia says the Second Republic adopted a tricolour variant for a few days, 24 February to 5 March 1848, and captions Philippoteaux's painting as depicting the rejection of the red flag in front of the city hall. FOTW says a decree of 7 March 1848 confirmed the tricolour ensign.
era-1848.open: Wikipedia does not describe the variant. The painting is cited as depicting Lamartine, not as a document.

era-1830.says: Wikipedia says Louis-Philippe restored the tricolour in 1830 and that it has been used since except in 1848. FOTW says the tricolour had been banned since 1815, reappeared during the July days of 1830, that on 30 July Lafayette gave Louis-Philippe a tricolour on the city hall balcony, that on 1 August 1830 his ordinance stated that the French nation resumes its colours, and that he used a fleur-de-lis coat of arms from 13 August 1830 to 16 February 1831 before dropping it.
era-1830.open: FOTW's July Monarchy page does not cover the cockade, military flags with the Gallic cock or 1848.

era-1814.says: FOTW says the white flag was restored as the national flag in 1814, which it had not been under the Ancien Régime (Sache). Wikipedia says the tricolour was replaced by the pre-revolutionary white naval flag in 1815–1830. FOTW says that on landing from Elba in 1815 Napoléon had the tricolour hoisted, that a decree of 9 March 1815 ordered the tricolour displayed on town halls, and that the Hundred Days ended at Waterloo on 18 June 1815.
era-1814.open: The sources differ on 1814 or 1815 for the white flag. FOTW's Restoration page gives no decree and does not cover the white cockade or royal standards. This page draws the plain white flag, without arms.

era-1804.says: Flags of the World: Napoleon was proclaimed Emperor on 2 December 1804, the national flag during the First Empire was the blue-white-red tricolour (Sache), the bee served as an imperial symbol from 1804 to 1814 and in the Hundred Days, and Napoleon had no personal standard before Elba. Wikipedia: 'Under Napoleon I, the proportions were changed to make the stripes' width equal', and after his defeat the Bourbon restoration (1815) replaced the tricolour with a white flag.
era-1804.open: Wikipedia gives no date for the change of proportions under Napoleon I and does not mention eagle standards or the bees; the 'imperial emblems beside it' rest on FOTW alone, and no decree confirming the flag was read.

era-1789.says: Wikipedia says the cockade was adopted in July 1789, Paris militia wearing blue and red with white added, that it became part of the National Guard uniform on 27 July 1789, that the Constituent Assembly approved a vertical red-white-blue tricolour on 24 October 1790, and that a resolution of 15 February 1794 reversed the order to blue-white-red. FOTW says the cockade existed by 12 July 1789, that the navy's jack and ensign of 1790 were the first vertical tricolours with red at the hoist, that a decree of 24 October 1790 became law on 31 October, that a decree of 26 June 1793 ordered tricolour flags on Paris public buildings, and that the decree of 15 February 1794 (27 Pluviôse, Year II) set blue at the hoist.
era-1789.open: Wikipedia says the attribution of the white is disputed, and FOTW calls the story of the king pinning the cockade a legend. The 1790 decree was about the flag generally, not only ships. The drawing shows the 1794 order.

era-1589.says: Wikipedia says the House of Bourbon ruled France in 1589–1792 and 1815–1848 and that the white Bourbon banner was used (image caption). FOTW says white was the royal and military colour, that the King's vessels carried plain white flags (Gay), and that a decree of 3 March 1781 prescribed the white flag on French consulates in the Levant, the first reported use of a white flag on land.
era-1589.open: FOTW says the white flag was a command flag and was not the national flag until 1814. Neither source describes a specific Bourbon royal standard.

era-987.says: Wikipedia says the red oriflamme, the banner of Saint Denis, was the royal banner under the Capetians; that the Valois arms of 1328 were blue with gold fleurs-de-lis bordered in red; that Charles V reduced the lilies to three about 1376; and that the blue field became the common standard of French armies in the Hundred Years' War. FOTW says the lilies first appear on Louis VIII's seal and on Philip II's banners (Gay), that Charles V reduced them to three in 1365, that a blue pendon with three gold fleurs-de-lis is described in 1350, and that in 1422 Charles VII adopted a white flag as his banner.
era-987.open: The date of the reduction to three lilies differs (1365 or about 1376). The oriflamme, which Wikipedia says was the royal banner under the Capetians, is not drawn, and the image shows the later blue banner for the whole span.

era-481.says: This page's own caption calls the image a placeholder: «placeholder maroon field — no flag documented for the Frankish kingdoms».
era-481.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-58bce.says: This page's own caption calls the image a placeholder: «placeholder maroon field — no flag documented for Gaul».
era-58bce.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1898.says: Wikipedia and FOTW: a Royal Decree of 13 October 1843 made the red-yellow-red flag the State and war flag and ensign. FOTW (War Ensign 1785-1931): the red-yellow-red flag with the crowned arms was the war ensign from 1785 and the state flag from 1843; the page notes a 1899 depiction. The U.S. National Park Service says the red-and-gold ensign replaced the Burgundian cross at sea in 1785 and as regimental colours in 1843.
era-1898.open: Three sources agree that the red-yellow-red flag, not the Cross of Burgundy, was Spain's state and war flag in 1898, so the page's drawing is contradicted and should be replaced; no source read says the cross flew in the Spanish-American War.

era-1808.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Spain): the red-yellow flag spread among people and volunteers from 1808 and became the colours of the Cortes de Cadiz; the red-yellow-red ensign dates from 1785. FOTW (War Ensign 1785-1931): the red-yellow-red ensign with crowned arms was the war ensign from the Royal Decree of 25 May 1785 and the state and war flag from 1843. FOTW (Kingdom of Spain 1808-1813), quoting a Spanish Navy page: during the Peninsular War white predominated but some corps used red and yellow flags popularised by Cadiz; Joseph Bonaparte's regime used a white flag with new arms.
era-1808.open: The sources confirm the red-yellow-red ensign for Spain in this period, not that it was flown in each rebel or loyalist territory; Joseph I's white flag of 1808-13 and the many local flags of the independence wars are not shown on the page, and the '1810-1825' label and the 1830s end are not covered.

era-1580.says: FOTW (Burgundy Cross Flag 1506-1785): the red Burgundy saltire raguly on white was Spain's ensign from 1506 to the 1670s, thereafter a jack until 1785, and the Spanish military flag from the 16th century to 1843. FOTW (1701-1785): Charles II and Philip V replaced it as ensign with royal arms on white. Wikipedia: Philip V's naval ensign was white with royal arms, the red-yellow-red ensign replaced it by 1785. NPS: the white flag with the red Burgundian saltire was flown by Spanish ships and fortresses across the New World until the 1785 ensign.
era-1580.open: The cross was the ensign only to the 1670s; for the rest of 1580-1808 the sources describe it as a jack and military flag, with royal arms on white and, from 1785, red-yellow-red as the ensign. FOTW also says it was never the official flag of the Empire, which was properly the royal standard. The gold medallion in the page's drawing is not supported.

era-1535.says: Wikipedia (Cross of Burgundy): the cross served as the flag of the viceroyalties, and New Spain's viceregal banner lasted to 24 August 1821. FOTW: the saltire was Spain's ensign from 1506 and its military flag in the 16th century, and a contributor calls it a military banner rather than the empire's official flag. NPS: this was the flag carried by ships and flown over the fortresses guarding Spain's New World possessions.
era-1535.open: No source gives the viceroyalties' founding dates (1535 for New Spain, 1542 for Peru) or says the cross was a viceroyalty's own flag in the 1535-1580s; FOTW says explicitly that it was never the official flag of the Empire, so 'naval and military ensign' is supported but 'imperial flag' is not.

era-1519.says: Wikipedia: under Charles I (1516-56) Spanish armies used the Cross of Burgundy on different fields, the official one white; the earliest Spanish use dates to 1506 or after 1496. FOTW (Spain 1506-1700): the cross was 'the flag, if any was' carried by the conquistadors; Magellan 'most probably' used it. FOTW (Cortés): chroniclers (Tapia, Mendieta, Gómara) describe Cortés' flag as a red cross on white-and-blue flames with the motto 'In hoc signo' or a standard with the royal arms and a cross; the standard kept at Chapultepec is red with the Virgin Mary.
era-1519.open: The Cross of Burgundy is not what the chroniclers quoted by FOTW describe for Cortés; nothing read mentions Pizarro's flag. The link between the page's drawing and the conquest expeditions is contradicted for Cortés and unconfirmed for Pizarro.

era-1492.says: Wikipedia: a pennant of the Catholic Monarchs used until 1492 (file name 1475-1492); Aragonese and Castilian arms merged in 1475 (citation needed). FOTW (15th Century Flags): the Royal Standard of the Catholic Kings 1492-1506 is a white flag with their arms, quarterly Castile-León and Aragon-Sicily; Columbus' captains' ensigns were white with a green cross and the crowned letters F and Y, from his logbook.
era-1492.open: The sources describe a white flag with the Catholic Kings' arms, not the red field with coloured blocks drawn on the page, which is a schematic reconstruction without a source. Some authors cited by FOTW suggest the royal banner of Castile and León was flown instead.

era-30bce.says: Wikipedia's article on Roman Egypt says Egypt was ruled as the imperial province of Aegyptus from its conquest by Roman forces in 30 BC to AD 642, and its Ptolemaic Kingdom article says the dynasty ruled until the death of Cleopatra VII in 30 BC. The World History Encyclopedia (Wasson) says Egypt became the property of Rome after Cleopatra VII's death in 30 BCE, ending the Ptolemaic dynasty. The flag articles originally read (Wikipedia's History of flags, FOTW's Egypt page) do not cover the annexation.
era-30bce.open: The annexation is established, but no source read says anything about a flag or emblem for the event; the later Roman and Byzantine, Islamic and modern story on this page is carried by the Egypt page and was not checked here. Egypt's governance as the emperor's personal domain rather than an ordinary province is a nuance not covered.

era-305bce.says: A National Museums Liverpool catalogue record of a coin of Ptolemy I Soter (king of Egypt from about 305 or 306 BC) describes the obverse as a diademed head of Ptolemy I with aegis and the reverse as an eagle with closed wings standing on a thunderbolt; Wikipedia's Ptolemaic Kingdom article gives the dynasty's span as Ptolemy I until Cleopatra VII's death in 30 BC. Wikipedia's History of flags and FOTW's Egypt page say nothing of the period.
era-305bce.open: The diadem and the eagle on a thunderbolt are established on Ptolemaic coinage; their use on standards and the claim that Ptolemies kept pharaonic crowns and the uraeus in temple contexts are not established by the pages read. A search hit from National Museums Scotland returned a 403 and was not used.

era-664bce.says: Wikipedia's Late Period article: 664-332 BC, from the Saite 26th Dynasty of Psamtik I through later native dynasties, including Achaemenid rule from the conquest by Cambyses II in 525 BC, ending with Alexander the Great and Ptolemy I. Wikipedia's Pschent article and the Egypt Exploration Society's resource describe the double crown as the emblem of unified rule from the First Dynasty on.
era-664bce.open: The period's native and Persian rule is established, but no source read documents the Pschent as a royal emblem in the Late Period or under Persian kings, and the red-field reconstruction is not covered.

era-1077bce.says: Wikipedia's Third Intermediate Period article: the period began with the death of Ramesses XI in 1077 BC and ran to about 664 BC and Psamtik I, after the Nubian Kushite 25th Dynasty was driven out by the Assyrians. It confirms the political fragmentation (Libyan and Nubian dynasties) but no source read describes an emblem or banner for the period.
era-1077bce.open: The absence of a single documented banner is not a finding; no royal-emblem source for the Libyan and Nubian dynasties was read. A Libyan or Kushite royal emblem source (for example museum material on Shoshenq or Taharqa) was not found.

era-1550bce.says: The Carnegie Museum of Natural History's catalogue entry for a cobra head carved about 1345-1347 BCE at Akhenaten's capital (accession 7043-5, bought from the Egypt Exploration Society in 1922): cobras represented Wadjet, a protective goddess connected to kingship, and the cobra heads were set into sun disk decorations. The Egypt Exploration Society's resource on royal crowns: the Wadjet cobra is sometimes shown on the forehead of kings, illustrated by New Kingdom reliefs of Ahmose and Seti I, and the Khepresh crown was adopted by many later 18th Dynasty kings.
era-1550bce.open: 'Most consistently attested' is a superlative neither source states, and neither says the uraeus or sun-disk was a banner or flag; the page shows a reconstruction of a royal device. The EES resource does not date the uraeus on kings' brows to the New Kingdom alone.

era-1650bce.says: Wikipedia's Second Intermediate Period article: Egypt divided into smaller dynasties between the Middle and New Kingdoms (it dates the period from 1782 BC); the Hyksos 15th Dynasty ruled from Avaris. Neither it nor the flag sources read describe an emblem for the Hyksos or the Theban kings.
era-1650bce.open: The political split is confirmed, but the claim that no emblem is securely documented is an absence, not a finding, and no Hyksos or Theban emblem source was read; Wikipedia's start date (1782 BC) differs from this row's c. 1650.

era-2055bce.says: Wikipedia's Pschent article: the double crown combined the White Hedjet of Upper Egypt and the Red Deshret of Lower Egypt and represented the pharaoh's power over all of unified Egypt; attributed to the First Dynasty (Menes), with Djet the first known wearer, and the Palermo Stone gives it to First Dynasty and later pharaohs; no Pschent survives. The Egypt Exploration Society's resource says the double crown symbolises the unification of Lower and Upper Egypt under one ruler.
era-2055bce.open: Both sources establish the Pschent as the emblem of unified rule, but neither documents it for the Middle Kingdom (c. 2055-1650 BCE) specifically, and the wording 'from this era forward' understates its much earlier origin in the First Dynasty.

era-2181bce.says: Wikipedia's First Intermediate Period article: c. 2181-2055 BC after the Old Kingdom, 'very little monumental evidence survives', with the Eighth to Tenth and part of the Eleventh Dynasties; no emblem or banner is described in the pages read.
era-2181bce.open: The fragmented political picture is supported but the statement that no unified royal emblem survives is an absence not a finding; no source on nomarch or Herakleopolitan royal emblems was read.

era-2686bce.says: Livius.org: the serekh was the ruler's most important name in the first dynasties, and Fourth Dynasty kings (within the Old Kingdom) stressed names written in cartouches instead. Wikipedia's Serekh article: the serekh was used as a royal crest and predates the cartouche by four dynasties. The Egypt Exploration Society's resource describes the Hedjet and Deshret crowns of Upper and Lower Egypt and their combination as the double crown.
era-2686bce.open: No source read documents the crowns or serekh for the Old Kingdom as a period, and Livius indicates the serekh lost prominence from the Fourth Dynasty, so 'royal iconography centres on the serekh' fits the Third Dynasty better than the whole span; the pyramid-gold field and monumental-authority wording are the page's own.

era-3100bce.says: Wikipedia's Serekh article: the serekh is a rectangular enclosure representing a palace facade, surmounted by (usually) the Horus falcon, indicating that the text inside is a royal name; it was the earliest convention for setting apart the royal name, predating the cartouche by four dynasties, and appears from the Gerzeh culture (c. 3400 BC). Livius.org (Lendering): in the first dynasties the ruler's most important name was written in the serekh, topped by a falcon thought to be Horus, e.g. on cups of Djer (Narmer's second successor) and an axe blade of Aha. Wikipedia's History of flags separately says the Narmer Palette is said to show the earliest standards.
era-3100bce.open: Neither source ties the serekh to Narmer's unification as a flag or banner; both treat it as a name-frame, so 'earliest royal identifying emblem' holds for the royal-name convention, and Wikipedia dates its first appearance (c. 3400 BC) before this row's 3100 BCE start. Livius says the falcon as Horus is likely but cannot be proved.

era-1975.says: Wikipedia: the kingdom's flag lost official status 1975; government banner is the state emblem on white. FOTW: Sikkim became India's 22nd state in 1975; no official state flag; SDF flag de facto.
era-1975.open: Neither source says India's tricolour is Sikkim's state flag; that claim is uncovered.

era-1947.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Sikkim): a khorlo with gankyil on every flag of the kingdom from 1877 to 1975 and a simpler design with a solid red border from 1967; its Kingdom of Sikkim article shows a state flag (1967-1975) and a royal flag (1877-1975) for the kingdom. Flags of the World: c.1914-1962 a white field with a triple red, white and blue border and a red circular emblem (Carr 1961); 1962-1967 a red wheel with six motifs (Barraclough 1965); and a pre-merger flag of white with a red border and a yellow chakra (Barraclough).
era-1947.open: The drawing on this page is a reconstruction, as Wikipedia says of its images, and the two sources differ in detail on the emblem and colours. Neither gives dates for the Indian protectorate itself, or describes a maroon field or crossed dorje (which this page no longer claims).

era-1861.says: Wikipedia: the first Sikkimese flag was adopted in 1877, every flag of the kingdom bore a khorlo and gankyil, and its images of the 1877-1975 royal flag are reconstructions; its Kingdom of Sikkim article lists the royal flag as 1877-1975. Flags of the World: an 1877-c.1914 flag at 2:3 whose design is not described, and a c.1914-1962 flag, about 7:9, white with a triple border and red circular emblem (Carr 1961).
era-1861.open: There was no Sikkimese flag for 1861-1877 (Wikipedia has the Union Jack to 1877), so the flag is established for 1877-1947 only. The 1877-c.1914 design is described by neither source, and the maroon-and-gold banner is not supported. The British protectorate's dates are not given.

era-1642.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Sikkim): Nepalese, Bhutanese and Tibetan banners until 1816, the Union Jack to 1877, first Sikkimese flag 1877. Wikipedia's Kingdom of Sikkim article shows no flag before the royal flag of 1877. Flags of the World's Sikkim page starts with the 1877 flag.
era-1642.open: No source read gives a Namgyal-period flag for 1642-1861, so the maroon-and-gold dorje banner remains an unsupported reconstruction; the silence is not proof that none existed.
